title: One world ocean
description: Earth has one connected global ocean, divided into named regions. It covers more than 70% of the surface and holds about 97% of Earth's water.

facts.text: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, and the ocean alone covers more than 70% of the planet's surface.
There is only one global ocean; the named oceans are regions of it, divided by lines people drew rather than walls of land.
About 97% of Earth's water is in the ocean (USGS puts it at about 96.5%).

title: Why all life depends on the ocean
description: The ocean supplies about half of Earth's oxygen, made by plankton, and almost all the rain that falls on land starts off as ocean water.

facts.text: About half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean, mostly made by plankton: drifting plants, algae and some bacteria that photosynthesize.
The ocean supplies most of the water that evaporates into the air; winds carry the vapor, and it falls again as rain and snow, over land as well as sea.

title: How deep the ocean goes
description: The ocean averages about 3,700 m deep and reaches about 11 km at its deepest, yet on a 30 cm globe it would be a film under a tenth of a millimeter deep.

facts.text: On December 7, 1972, the crew of Apollo 17 photographed the whole Earth while traveling to the Moon; the picture is known as the Blue Marble.
The ocean's average depth is about 3,682 m, roughly 3,700 m.
The ocean's deepest known point, Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, is about 10,935 m deep, roughly 11 km.
On a globe 30 cm across, the ocean's average depth would be under a tenth of a millimeter and its deepest point about a quarter millimeter (Earth's radius: 6,371 km).

title: The five named oceans by size
description: The Pacific is by far the largest ocean, then the Atlantic, Indian, Southern and, smallest, the Arctic.

facts.text: Historically there were four named oceans: the Atlantic, Pacific, Indian and Arctic.
The Pacific is by far the largest ocean basin: it holds more than half of the free water on Earth, and all the continents could fit into it.
After the Pacific, the ocean basins rank by size as the Atlantic, the Indian, the Southern and, smallest, the Arctic.

title: The Southern Ocean: defined by a current
description: The Southern Ocean is bounded by the Antarctic Circumpolar Current at about 60° S. NOAA and National Geographic recognize it; the IHO's position has shifted.

facts.text: Unlike the other oceans, defined by the continents around them, the Southern Ocean is defined by a current that circles Antarctica; its northern edge is set at 60° S.
The US Board on Geographic Names has used the name Southern Ocean since 1999, NOAA counts it as the fifth ocean, and National Geographic began recognizing it on June 8, 2021.

The International Hydrographic Organization, which publishes the standard limits of oceans and seas, dropped the Southern Ocean in 1953 and voted to recognize it again in 2023, without binding members' views.

title: The fingerprint test for Earth's water
description: The ratio of heavy hydrogen (deuterium) in water is a clue to where it came from. Comet 67P seemed a mismatch in 2014; asteroid meteorites matched.

facts.text: Scientists long thought any water present as Earth formed would have evaporated or been blown off into space, so it must have arrived later, on comets or icy asteroids.
Deuterium is a rare, heavier form of hydrogen that forms more readily in cold places far from the Sun, so water's share of it is a clue to where that water formed.
In 2014, ESA's Rosetta found comet 67P's water had a deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio more than three times that of Earth's oceans, so comets like it looked unlikely as the main source.
Water in meteorites called carbonaceous chondrites, pieces of asteroids, matches Earth's hydrogen fingerprint; a 2014 WHOI-led study concluded Earth got its water early from such bodies.

title: Earth's water: a debated mix
description: Newer work reopened the case: 67P's water may match Earth's after all, and Earth's own building blocks may have carried water. The shares remain debated.

facts.text: In 2024, a NASA-led team found that dust had skewed Rosetta's readings, and that comet 67P's water has a signature similar to the water in Earth's oceans.
A 2020 study found that enstatite chondrite meteorites, like the material Earth formed from, hold enough hydrogen to supply at least three times the water in Earth's oceans.
Some of Earth's water came from vapor vented by volcanoes, and a substantial portion from asteroids and possibly comets; how much came from each is still debated.

title: How salty the sea is
description: Seawater averages about 35 parts per thousand salt, mostly chloride and sodium, enough salt to bury the land about 40 stories deep.

facts.text: If the ocean's salt were removed and spread evenly over Earth's land, it would form a layer about as tall as a 40-story office building.
Seawater's average salinity is about 35 parts per thousand: dissolved salts make up about 3.5% of its weight.
Chloride and sodium, the two parts of table salt, are the most common dissolved ions in seawater and make up most of them.

title: Where sea salt comes from
description: Slightly acidic rain weathers rock, rivers carry the salts to sea, and evaporation leaves them behind. Hydrothermal vents and undersea eruptions add more from below.

facts.text: Rain holds dissolved carbon dioxide, which makes it slightly acidic, so it breaks down rocks on land; streams and rivers carry the released salts to the ocean.
When ocean water evaporates the salts are left behind, so salt builds up in the sea; river water carries dissolved salt too, but far too little to taste.
Some ocean salts come from below: seawater heated by magma in the sea floor gushes from hydrothermal vents with dissolved minerals, and undersea eruptions release minerals too.

title: Seawater stacks by density
description: Cold and salty water is denser than warm and fresh water, so the ocean sorts itself: light water on top, dense water below.

facts.text: At 10°C, a liter of fresh water weighs 1,000 g and a liter of seawater about 1,026 g, about 26 g more.
Cold water is denser than warm water, and salty water is denser than fresh water.
When waters of different density meet in the ocean, they order themselves from less dense near the surface to more dense at depth.

title: The thermocline
description: Between warm surface water and cold deep water lies the thermocline, where temperature drops fast with depth. It varies from tropics to poles.

facts.text: A thermocline is the transition layer between warmer mixed water at the ocean's surface and much colder deep water, where temperature drops rapidly with depth.
The thermocline is semi-permanent in the tropics, changes with the seasons in temperate seas, and is shallow or missing in polar seas.

title: Why the ocean is blue
description: Water absorbs red light and scatters blue back, so a deep body of water looks blue. A glass looks clear, and sky reflection only matters at the surface.

facts.text: Water absorbs colors at the red end of the spectrum much more strongly than blue, like a filter, and scatters the remaining blue light back toward our eyes.
Water has a faint blue color of its own, caused by slight absorption of red light, so a small amount such as a glass looks colorless.
The sea's surface does reflect the sky, which is why big bodies of water look gray on overcast days, but the color of the sea and of the sky arise separately.

title: Why some seas look green
description: Particles, sediments and phytoplankton change the sea's color: light bounces off particles, and chlorophyll absorbs some colors, tinting water green.

facts.text: Seawater can look green or other colors where light bounces off sediments and particles, or where phytoplankton, whose chlorophyll absorbs some colors, are plentiful.

title: Colors fade in order underwater
description: Water absorbs the longest wavelengths first: red and orange vanish within a few meters, then yellow and green; blue and violet reach deepest.

facts.text: A few meters underwater most red and orange light is gone; yellow and green fade next, and blue and violet reach deepest.
At 100 m, red light does not penetrate, so a red fish looks blackish: there is no red light for it to reflect.

title: How deep sunlight reaches
description: Below about 200 m there is too little light for photosynthesis, and below 1,000 m no sunlight arrives at all.

facts.text: There is rarely significant light below about 200 m in the ocean, too little for photosynthesis, though faint light may be detected down to 1,000 m.
Sunlight does not reach ocean depths below 1,000 m.
With an average depth of about 3,700 m and no sunlight below 1,000 m, a typical sea floor lies about 2,700 m below the last sunlight, nearly three quarters of the way down.

title: Pressure grows with depth
description: Every 10 m of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure: double the surface pressure at 10 m, about 200 atmospheres at 2,000 m.

facts.text: Pressure in the ocean increases by about one atmosphere, the pressure of the air at sea level, for every 10 m of depth.
At 10 m down, the pressure on a diver is double what it is at the surface.
Water adds about 10 atmospheres of pressure at 100 m and about 200 atmospheres at 2,000 m.

title: Pressure crushes air spaces
description: Water barely compresses but air does, so deep pressure crushes the air pockets in a foam cup, and would collapse air spaces like human lungs.

facts.text: Oceanographers send decorated foam cups into the deep; pressure squeezes the tiny air pockets in the foam, and the cups come back shrunken for good.
Water is nearly incompressible, but air is not: enough pressure would collapse air-filled spaces such as human lungs and the air spaces in our heads.

title: All Earth's water in one ball
description: Gathered into one sphere, all of Earth's water would be about 1,385 km across, well under half the Moon's width.

facts.text: If all of Earth's water, about 1,386 million cubic km, were gathered into one ball, it would be about 1,385 km across.
A 1,385 km ball of water would be well under half as wide as the Moon, which has a radius of about 1,740 km.

title: Mapping the sea floor with sound
description: Light can't reach the deep floor, so people mapped it first with weighted ropes, then with sonar: time a sound's echo off the bottom. Multibeam sonar maps a wide fan at once.

facts.text: We have better maps of Mars than of Earth's seafloor, because light can't get through deep seawater, so the tools that map land from above can't see the bottom.
In the early 1800s, mariners measured seafloor depth with lead lines, weighted ropes; each drop gave the depth at a single point, so surveys were slow and laborious.
Sonar, developed in the 1920s, measures seafloor depth by sending out a sound and timing how long its echo takes to return from the bottom.
Sound travels far through seawater, which is why the deep seafloor is mapped with sound rather than light.
Multibeam sonar, developed in the 1960s, sends many beams of sound at once in a fan shape, mapping a wide strip of seafloor under the ship and out to each side.

title: How much of the sea floor is mapped
description: When Seabed 2030 launched in 2017, only about 6% of the ocean floor was mapped in modern detail. By April 2026 the figure was 28.7%, with the whole floor the goal for 2030.

facts.text: As of April 2026, the Seabed 2030 project reported that 28.7% of the world's ocean floor had been mapped in modern detail.
The Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 project, launched in 2017 when only about 6% of the ocean floor was mapped to modern standards, aims to map the entire ocean floor by 2030.

title: Continental shelves
description: A continental shelf is the shallow, gently sloping underwater edge of a continent, usually 100 to 200 m deep, ending at the shelf break where the steep continental slope begins.

facts.text: A continental shelf is the broad, shallow, gently sloping underwater edge of a continent, running from the shore out to a sudden drop called the shelf break.
Continental shelves typically extend from the coast to depths of about 100 to 200 m.
A continental shelf slopes seaward at an average of only about 0.1 degree, a drop of under 2 m for every kilometer.
Beyond the shelf break, the much steeper continental slope drops toward the deep ocean floor.
Continental shelves vary greatly in width: narrow or almost absent along some coasts, while the largest, off Siberia, extends about 1,500 km into the Arctic Ocean.
Continental shelves make up only about 8% of the area covered by the ocean.

title: Why shelves are full of life
description: Shelf water is shallow enough for sunlight to power photosynthesis, and rivers wash in nutrients, so the shelves support abundant sea life and rich fisheries.

facts.text: Because shelf water is shallow, sunlight reaches through it to support photosynthesis, and river runoff brings nutrients, so continental shelves support abundant sea life and rich fish populations.

title: The mid-ocean ridge
description: Earth's longest mountain range, about 65,000 km long and about 90% underwater, is a chain of thousands of volcanoes where plates pull apart and magma rises.

facts.text: The mid-ocean ridge system winds about 65,000 km around the globe, like the stitches on a baseball, making it Earth's longest mountain range.
About 90% of the mid-ocean ridge system lies under the ocean.
The mid-ocean ridge is the largest single volcanic feature on Earth, made of thousands of volcanoes and volcanic ridge segments that erupt from time to time.
Mid-ocean ridges rise from sea floor about 5 km deep to crests about 2.6 km below the surface.
At a mid-ocean ridge, plates push apart and magma rises to fill the gap, building new sea floor.

title: Marie Tharp finds the rift
description: In 1952 Marie Tharp, plotting echo soundings, found a valley down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Bruce Heezen scoffed until earthquakes lined up inside it.

facts.text: In 1952, Marie Tharp, turning echo soundings of the Atlantic floor into profiles at Columbia University's Lamont lab, found a V-shaped valley running down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Her colleague Bruce Heezen at first dismissed the valley as "girl talk"; by 1953 he was convinced, when earthquake locations turned out to line up inside it.

title: Ocean trenches
description: Trenches are long, narrow, very deep gashes where one plate is pushed beneath another. Most are in the Pacific; the Mariana Trench holds Challenger Deep.

facts.text: Ocean trenches form by subduction: where plates converge, the older, denser plate is pushed down beneath the lighter one and plunges into the mantle.
Trenches are long, narrow and very deep, and most of them are in the Pacific Ocean.
The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped trench about 2,550 km long and about 69 km wide on average.
The Tonga, Kuril-Kamchatka, Philippine and Kermadec Trenches also reach depths greater than 10,000 m.
Mount Everest stands about 8,849 m tall; set on the floor of Challenger Deep, about 10,935 m down, its peak would still be about 2 km underwater.
At Challenger Deep, about 10,935 m down, the water adds more than 1,000 atmospheres of pressure.
Earthquakes in subduction zones caused the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2011 Tohoku tsunami in Japan.

title: Seamounts
description: Seamounts are steep underwater mountains at least 1,000 m tall, mostly extinct volcanoes. There are more than 100,000, and less than 0.1% have been explored.

facts.text: A seamount is a steep-sided underwater mountain rising at least 1,000 m above the surrounding sea floor; most are extinct volcanoes.
Scientists estimate there are more than 100,000 seamounts, and less than one-tenth of a percent of them have been explored.

title: Islands born from seamounts
description: An undersea volcano that grows tall enough breaks the surface as an island, as Surtsey did in 1963. Waves wear islands down; guyots are old islands planed flat and sunk.

facts.text: Surtsey, off Iceland's south coast, was born in a volcanic eruption that began on the sea floor about 130 m down and broke the surface in November 1963.
Surtsey's eruptions lasted about three and a half years; since then, waves have worn away almost half of its area (from about 2.5 to 1.4 square km by 2008).

Guyots are flat-topped seamounts: they began as volcanic islands near ridge crests, waves planed their tops flat, and they sank as the sea floor moved away from the ridge; most summits now lie 1,000 to 2,000 m down.

title: Hydrothermal vents: hot springs of the sea floor
description: Seawater seeps into cracks near spreading ridges, is heated by magma and gushes back out at up to about 400 degrees C, kept from boiling by the deep ocean's pressure.

facts.text: Hydrothermal vents were first observed in 1977, on a spreading ridge near the Galapagos Islands, where warm, chemical-rich fluid flowed from the Pacific sea floor, surrounded by unexpected communities of life.
At a hydrothermal vent, seawater seeps down through cracks in the ocean crust, is heated by magma below, and rises back out as a hot spring; most vents are along mid-ocean ridges.
Vent fluid can reach about 400°C, four times the 100°C at which water boils at sea level, yet it does not boil, because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

title: Black smokers
description: When hot vent fluid meets near-freezing seawater, its dissolved minerals solidify: black iron sulfide 'smoke' and chimneys that can grow tens of meters tall.

facts.text: When hot vent fluid meets near-freezing seawater, dissolved minerals solidify: black iron sulfide particles pour out like smoke, and the minerals build chimneys that can grow tens of meters tall.

title: Marine snow and ooze
description: A slow shower of organic bits, marine snow, sinks to the deep; what isn't eaten piles up as ooze over about three-quarters of the deep floor, only about 6 m per million years.

facts.text: Marine snow is a shower of organic material, such as bits of dead plants and animals and fecal matter, plus sand, soot and dust, falling from upper waters to the deep ocean; flakes can be several centimeters across and take weeks to reach the floor.
Uneaten marine snow piles up on the floor as ooze; ooze and other slow-settling deep-sea sediments cover about three-quarters of the deep ocean floor.
Deep-sea ooze builds up by only about 6 m per million years, about half a millimeter in 80 years.
Deep-sea mud counts as ooze when more than 30% of it is the tiny shells and skeletons of microscopic sea life, made of calcium carbonate or silica; with less, it is called deep-sea clay or red clay.

title: Abyssal plains
description: Abyssal plains, 3,000 to 6,000 m deep, are flat because sediment has filled in an older, hilly floor. Their depth changes by only 10 to 100 cm per kilometer.

facts.text: Abyssal plains are flat stretches of sea floor 3,000 to 6,000 m deep where sediment has filled in and smoothed an older, hilly floor; their depth changes by only 10 to 100 cm per kilometer.

title: The sea floor's conveyor belt
description: New ocean floor forms at the ridges and old floor sinks back at the trenches, so no sea floor is older than about 200 million years on a 4.5-billion-year-old planet.

facts.text: In 1960, geophysicist Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading: new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and old ocean floor sinks back into the trenches, so the ocean basins are constantly recycled and Earth doesn't get bigger.
Ocean floor is youngest at the ridge crests and older farther away; very little is older than 150 million years, and the oldest known, about 200 million years old, lies in the far western Pacific.
Earth is about 4.5 billion years old (USGS gives 4.54 billion).
Ocean-floor rocks are much younger than continental rocks.

title: Magnetic stripes on the sea floor
description: Cooling lava locks in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, which has flipped many times, so the floor carries mirror-image stripes on both sides of each ridge.

facts.text: As lava cools into rock, grains of the magnetic mineral magnetite lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field, so the ocean crust is a natural 'tape recording' of the field.

The ocean floor shows stripes of rock with alternating magnetic direction, running parallel to the mid-ocean ridge and matching on either side of it, because Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times.

title: How tsunamis cross oceans
description: A tsunami moves the whole water column, and its speed depends on depth: over the deep ocean it can pass 800 km/h and cross an ocean in less than a day.

facts.text: A tsunami from Alaska's Aleutian Islands reaches Hawaii in about five hours.
Unlike wind waves, which stir only the top layer of the ocean, a tsunami moves the entire water column, from the surface to the sea floor.
A tsunami's speed depends on water depth, faster in deeper water: over the deep ocean it can move as fast as a jet plane, over 800 km/h, and cross an entire ocean in less than a day.

title: Catching tsunamis on the sea floor
description: NOAA's DART stations put pressure recorders on the sea floor; a passing tsunami changes the water overhead, and they can sense one as small as 1 cm in 6,000 m of water.

facts.text: NOAA's DART stations use pressure recorders on the sea floor that sense changes in the water overhead and can detect a tsunami as small as 1 cm in 6,000 m of water.

title: The ocean floor, drained
description: NASA's drained-ocean animation reveals the floor in order: shelves by 140 m, ridges at 2,000 to 3,000 m, and by 6,000 m only the trenches still hold water.

facts.text: In 2008, NASA released an animation that lowers sea level step by step to reveal the sea floor, built from NOAA depth data.
In NASA's drained-ocean animation, the continental shelves are mostly exposed once sea level drops 140 m, except in the Arctic and Antarctic, where shelves are deeper.
In NASA's drained-ocean animation, the mid-ocean ridges start to appear when sea level drops 2,000 to 3,000 m.
By the time sea level drops 6,000 m in NASA's animation, most of the ocean is drained except the deep trenches.

title: How wind builds waves
description: Most waves are made by wind; how big they grow depends on wind speed, how long it blows and the fetch, and all three must combine.

facts.text: Most ocean waves are caused by wind, through friction between the wind and the water's surface.

Wind-wave size depends on wind speed, how long the wind blows, and the fetch (the distance over water it blows in one direction); large waves form only when all three combine, so a strong wind lasting only minutes, or a long blow over a short fetch, makes no large waves.

title: Waves move energy, water moves in circles
description: A wave carries energy, not water: surface water turns in circles about as wide as the wave is tall, and the circles fade out about half a wavelength down.

facts.text: Waves carry energy, not water, across the ocean: as a wave passes, the water moves in a circle rather than traveling with the wave.
Water near the surface moves in circular orbits about as wide as the wave is tall; the orbits shrink with depth, and below about half a wavelength the water is unaffected by the wave.

title: Swell crosses whole oceans
description: Waves that leave the wind that made them become swell, with smoother crests, and can cross an ocean with little energy lost, as Walter Munk showed in 1963.

facts.text: Waves that travel out of the area where they formed, no longer driven by the local wind, are called swell; swell has smoother crests than wind waves and can travel thousands of miles.

In 1963, Walter Munk of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography led a team that tracked swell from Antarctic storms more than 16,000 km across the Pacific, from New Zealand to Alaska; the waves lost very little energy on the way.
Waves with periods longer than about 10 or 12 seconds are arriving from a distant source and are considered swell.

title: Waves feel the bottom
description: In water shallower than about half a wavelength, a wave drags on the bottom, slows, bunches up and grows taller.

facts.text: When the water is shallower than about half a wave's length, the moving water drags along the bottom and its circular orbits flatten.
As a wave touches bottom it slows; the waves behind catch up, so the wavelength shortens, and with the same energy the wave grows taller.

title: Why waves break
description: Near shore, the bottom of a wave slows while the crest keeps going, so the wave steepens and topples, roughly where the water is 1.3 times as deep as the wave is tall.

facts.text: Near shore, friction with the bottom slows the lower part of a wave while the crest keeps its speed, so the wave steepens until the crest, with no water beneath it, topples forward as a breaker.
Waves generally become breakers where the water depth is about 1.3 times the wave height.
A wave also breaks when it gets too steep: when its height is more than about one-seventh of its wavelength.

title: What makes a wave rogue
description: A rogue wave is more than twice the size of the waves around it, unpredictable, often from an unexpected direction, and looks like a wall of water.

facts.text: Rogue waves are more than twice the size of surrounding waves, are very unpredictable, and often come from directions other than the prevailing wind and waves.
Rogue waves often look like walls of water, steep-sided with unusually deep troughs.
Rogue waves were part of sailors' folklore for centuries but have been accepted as real by scientists only in the past few decades.

title: The Draupner wave
description: On January 1, 1995, a laser on the Draupner platform in the North Sea measured a 25.6 m wave in seas of about 12 m, confirming rogue waves.

facts.text: On January 1, 1995, a downward-looking laser on the Draupner gas platform in the North Sea measured a wave 25.6 m high.
The significant wave height (roughly the average height of the highest third of waves) around the Draupner platform at the time was estimated at almost 12 m.
The Draupner measurement confirmed the existence of giant rogue waves, which had previously been reported only anecdotally by sailors.

title: How rogue waves form
description: Rogue waves form when crests of swells moving at different speeds and directions line up, or when storm waves run into an opposing current.

facts.text: When swells traveling at different speeds and directions coincide, their crests can reinforce each other, forming unusually large waves that quickly disappear.
Storm waves that run into an opposing current, as in the Gulf Stream or the Agulhas Current, can join into rogue waves, and these tend to last longer.

title: The Moon's two tidal bulges
description: The Moon's gravity raises two ocean bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the far side; Earth turns through both, so most shores get two high and two low tides a day.

facts.text: The Moon's gravity makes the oceans bulge on the side of Earth nearest the Moon and on the side farthest from it.
As Earth turns through the two bulges, most shorelines get two high tides and two low tides a day; one high tide to the next takes a little over 12 hours.

title: Tides run on lunar days
description: A lunar day is 24 hours and 50 minutes because Earth must turn extra to catch the orbiting Moon, so tides come about 50 minutes later each day.

facts.text: A lunar day, the time for a spot on Earth to come back under the Moon, is 24 hours and 50 minutes: the Moon orbits in the direction Earth spins, so Earth needs an extra 50 minutes to catch up, and the tides run about 50 minutes later each day.

title: One tide or two
description: Coasts get semidiurnal (two equal), mixed (two unequal) or diurnal (one) high tides per lunar day, depending on where they are.

facts.text: A semidiurnal tide brings two high and two low tides of about equal size each lunar day, a mixed tide two of different sizes, and a diurnal tide one high and one low.
Semidiurnal tides are common on North America's east coast, mixed tides on its west coast, and diurnal tides in many parts of the Gulf of Mexico.

title: The Sun's share of the tides
description: The Sun is far more massive than the Moon but about 390 times farther away, so its tidal force is a little less than half the Moon's.

facts.text: The Sun has about 27 million times the Moon's mass but is about 390 times farther away, which gives it a little less than half the Moon's tide-generating force.
Solar tides are about half as large as lunar tides and show up as a variation of the lunar tide pattern, not as a separate set of tides.

title: Spring and neap tides
description: At new and full moon the Sun and Moon line up for spring tides; about a week later, at the quarter moons, they pull at right angles for neap tides.

facts.text: Twice a month, at new and full moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine, making higher high tides and lower low tides: spring tides.
Spring tides are named for the tide 'springing forth' and have nothing to do with the season.

About seven days after a spring tide, at the first and third quarter moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and partly cancel, giving neap tides: highs a little lower and lows a little higher than average.

title: King tides
description: Once a month the Moon is closest to Earth (perigee) and raises bigger tides; together with a new or full moon, that brings the exceptionally high tides called king tides.

facts.text: Once a month, when the Moon is closest to Earth (perigee), tide-generating forces are higher than usual; 'king tide' is a popular, non-scientific name for exceptionally high tides, typically at a new or full moon.

title: The world's highest tides
description: NOAA places the world's highest tides in Canada's Bay of Fundy, at Burntcoat Head, where the tide can rise 16 m.

facts.text: NOAA says the highest tides in the world are in Canada's Bay of Fundy, at Burntcoat Head, Nova Scotia.
At the head of the Bay of Fundy the tide can rise 16 m, about the height of a four-story building.

title: Why Fundy sloshes so high
description: The Bay of Fundy's water rocks back and forth in about 13 hours, close to the tide's 12 h 25 min rhythm, so each tide pushes the sloshing higher.

facts.text: Water in the Bay of Fundy has a natural rocking motion (a seiche), like water sloshing in a bathtub, which rocks in seconds; one rock from the bay's mouth to its head and back takes about 13 hours.
The Atlantic tide flooding into the Bay of Fundy every 12 hours and 25 minutes reinforces the bay's rocking, like small, well-timed pushes on a swing.

title: Coastline shape sets tidal range
description: Tidal range depends on the shape of coasts and basins: narrow bays magnify tides, and northern continents crowding the ocean raise ranges, as near Anchorage.

facts.text: The Bay of Fundy's tide range is magnified by the bay's narrowness and shape.
Tidal range isn't set by latitude alone: in the northern high latitudes, North America, Europe and Asia are pressed close together, and this constriction of the ocean raises tidal ranges.
The highest tides in the United States are near Anchorage, Alaska, with tidal ranges averaging around 30 feet (about 9 m).

title: The four zones of the shore
description: The intertidal zone lies between high and low tide and stacks into bands: the spray zone, the high zone, the middle zone and the low zone.

facts.text: The intertidal zone is where the ocean meets the land between high and low tides; its middle zone is flooded and drained twice a day.
Rocky shores show vertical zonation: plants and animals are arranged in distinct horizontal layers.
The spray zone, above the high tide line, is dampened by ocean spray and covered by the sea only in extreme high tides or storms.
The high tide zone is underwater only at high tide, so it is hotter and drier; the middle zone is covered and uncovered for about equal amounts of time.
The low intertidal zone is almost always underwater, uncovered only during the lowest spring tides.
Barnacles, snails and limpets live in the high zone; mussels, sea stars and anemones in the middle zone; sea urchins in the low zone.

title: Surviving between the tides
description: Intertidal life must cope with changing moisture, temperature and salinity plus pounding waves; how much air exposure a species tolerates, and its predators and competitors, set where it lives.

facts.text: Anything living in the intertidal zone must survive changes in moisture, temperature and salinity and withstand strong waves.
The low tide zone has the greatest biodiversity of the intertidal zones, because it suits organisms that cannot tolerate air exposure for long.
Where a species lives in the intertidal zone depends on how well it tolerates underwater and above-water conditions, and on predators and competitors for space and food.

title: Tidal barrages
description: A tidal barrage dams a tidal basin, lets the rising tide in and releases it through turbines; La Rance in France (1966) and Sihwa Lake in South Korea are the big examples.

facts.text: A tidal barrage is a dam across a tidal basin: its gates let the rising tide fill the basin, then the trapped water is released through turbines as the tide falls.
The La Rance tidal power station, a barrage across the Rance estuary in Brittany, France, was inaugurated on November 26, 1966, and is still operating.
La Rance has 24 turbines and 240 MW of generating capacity.
The largest tidal power station is Sihwa Lake in South Korea, with 254 MW of capacity.
Producing tidal energy economically requires a tidal range of at least 10 feet (about 3 m).
A tidal barrage can change the tide level in the basin behind it, make the water murkier and block fish from moving in or out.

title: Tidal stream turbines
description: Tidal stream turbines work like underwater wind turbines in fast tidal currents, but must be much sturdier because water is about 800 times denser than air.

facts.text: Tidal turbines work like wind turbines, with blades turning a rotor, but water is about 800 times denser than air, so they must be much sturdier and heavier.
Tidal stream systems put turbines in fast tidal currents, especially around islands and coasts.

title: Tides are predictable power
description: Unlike wind, tides are predictable, which makes tidal energy promising for steady, reliable electricity.

facts.text: Unlike wind, tides are predictable, which makes marine energy promising for stable, reliable electricity.

title: What makes a storm surge
description: A storm surge is the rise in sea level caused by a storm, mainly its winds pushing water ashore; shallow, gently sloping coasts and concave bays make it bigger.

facts.text: Storm surge is the rise in sea level caused solely by a storm, mainly by the storm's winds pushing water onshore.

In deep water, storm-driven water can circulate downward; in shallow coastal water the sea floor blocks it, so it moves up and inland, and gently sloping shelves and concave bays make the surge larger.

title: Storm tide: surge plus tide
description: The storm tide is the storm surge plus the normal tide, so a storm around a new or full moon brings the highest water.

facts.text: Storm tide is the total water level during a storm: the storm surge plus the normal astronomical tide.
Storm tides are highest when a storm strikes around a new or full moon, when tides are already at their biggest.

title: Storm surge: the deadliest part of a hurricane
description: Storm surge is the greatest threat to life in a hurricane; Katrina's surge reached 27.8 feet at Pass Christian and pushed miles inland.

facts.text: The greatest threat to life in a hurricane comes from storm surge.
The highest high-water mark of Hurricane Katrina's storm surge, in August 2005, was 27.8 feet (about 8.5 m) at Pass Christian, Mississippi.
Katrina's surge reached at least six miles (about 10 km) inland in many parts of coastal Mississippi, and up to 12 miles along bays and rivers.

title: Tides are waves too
description: Tides are very long-period waves driven by the Moon and Sun: the crest arriving is high tide, and the trough is low tide.

facts.text: Tides are very long-period waves that move through the oceans in response to forces from the Moon and Sun.
When the crest of the tide wave reaches a place, it is high tide; low tide comes with the wave's trough.

title: Wind drives surface currents
description: Winds drag the top layer of the sea along by friction, making surface currents; spilled bath toys in 1992 helped test a wind-based current model.

facts.text: In January 1992 a cargo ship lost thousands of plastic bath toys in the North Pacific; that November, beachcombers began finding them in Alaska.
Oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer and NOAA's James Ingraham used the toys' landings to test a computer model that works out surface currents from the winds.
Winds drive the currents at or near the ocean's surface: as wind blows, it drags the top layer of water along with it by friction.

title: The Coriolis effect bends currents
description: Earth's rotation deflects moving water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, as Nansen saw in drifting sea ice.

facts.text: Polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen noticed that sea ice drifted 20 to 40 degrees to the right of the wind, not straight downwind, and blamed Earth's rotation.
Earth's rotation deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern: the Coriolis effect, named after Gaspard Gustave de Coriolis.

title: Ocean gyres
description: Gyres are huge rotating systems of currents. The five major ones turn clockwise north of the equator and counterclockwise south of it.

facts.text: A gyre is a large system of rotating ocean currents; gyres span oceans and can be thousands of kilometers across.
There are five major gyres: the North and South Pacific, the North and South Atlantic, and the Indian Ocean subtropical gyres.
Gyres north of the equator turn clockwise, and gyres south of it turn counterclockwise.

title: The Gulf Stream
description: A warm, fast current running north along Florida and northeast across the Atlantic, carrying more water than all rivers; Franklin and Folger charted it.

facts.text: In the 1760s, British mail ships took as much as two weeks longer to sail west to New York than ships sailing a similar distance east.
In 1768 Benjamin Franklin, deputy postmaster general for the colonies, asked his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket captain and former whaler, why the mail was slow.
Whalers knew of a warm, strong current and used it, Folger explained, while the mail captains did not know it and sailed against it.
Folger sketched the current, Franklin printed the chart and named it the Gulph Stream, and it went to the mail ships in 1769 or 1770; the captains seem to have ignored it.
The Gulf Stream is a warm current that moves north along the coast of Florida, turns east off North Carolina and flows northeast across the Atlantic.
The Gulf Stream averages about 6.4 km/h and carries more water than all the world's rivers combined.

title: How the Gulf Stream warms Europe
description: The Gulf Stream carries heat north; its warm water heats the air, and westerly winds bring milder winters to places like Bergen, Norway.

facts.text: The Gulf Stream is the Atlantic's main conveyor of heat from south to north; in the cold far north its warm water heats the air above it.
Prevailing westerly winds carry the ocean's warmth and moisture onto northwestern Europe, giving it milder weather than other places as far north.
The warm Gulf Stream brings milder winter weather to Bergen, Norway, than to New York, which lies much further south.

title: The global ocean conveyor
description: Cold, salty water sinks in the far North Atlantic and drives a slow, density-driven circulation; one lap takes about 1,000 years.

facts.text: When sea ice forms, the salt does not freeze; it is left in the surrounding water, which becomes saltier and denser.
In the far North Atlantic, water chilled by Arctic air grows cold, salty and dense and sinks; surface water moves in to replace it, creating a current.
The deep, slow circulation is called thermohaline circulation because it is driven by density differences from temperature (thermo) and salinity (haline).
The global conveyor belt moves at a few centimeters per second, and any given cubic meter of water takes about 1,000 years to complete the journey.

title: The AMOC's outlook
description: The IPCC says the Atlantic overturning will very likely weaken this century, with low confidence in how much and medium confidence of no abrupt collapse before 2100.

facts.text: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), the Atlantic part of the conveyor, carries warm water from the tropics north into the North Atlantic.
Warming surface water and extra fresh water from rain and melting ice make the North Atlantic's surface water lighter, so less of it sinks, and models project the AMOC to weaken.
The IPCC (2021) says the AMOC will very likely weaken this century, with low confidence in how much, and medium confidence it will not collapse abruptly before 2100.

title: How El Niño works
description: When Pacific trade winds weaken, warm water spreads east, upwelling off South America weakens, and the central and eastern tropical Pacific warms.

facts.text: South American fishermen noticed warmer coastal water and poor fish catches around Christmas every few years, and nicknamed it El Niño, Spanish for little boy.
Normally, trade winds blow west along the equator, pushing warm surface water from South America toward Asia, and cold, nutrient-rich water rises off South America to replace it.
In an El Niño, the trade winds across the tropical Pacific are weaker than usual, and the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than average.
During El Niño, upwelling off South America weakens or stops, so fewer phytoplankton grow there, which affects the fish that eat them and everything that eats fish.
La Niña is the opposite phase; El Niño and La Niña episodes come every 2 to 7 years on average and typically last 9 to 12 months.

title: El Niño's reach
description: El Niño shifts weather far away, such as a wetter US Gulf Coast, and nudges global temperature up.

facts.text: During El Niño, the northern US and Canada tend to be drier and warmer than usual, while the US Gulf Coast and Southeast are wetter, with more flooding.
Because the Pacific is so big, El Niño nudges the whole planet's temperature: the warmest year of a decade tends to be an El Niño year.

title: Warm seas fuel hurricanes
description: Hurricanes need seawater of at least 26.5°C; evaporation and condensation turn that heat into wind, and storms weaken over land.

facts.text: Warm ocean water is the fuel of a hurricane's heat engine, which is why hurricanes form over tropical and subtropical waters.
A hurricane needs seawater of at least 26.5°C, and that warmth must reach down about 50 m.
Warm water evaporates into warm, moist air that rises into the storm; as it cools, the vapor condenses into clouds, releasing more heat that powers the storm.
Once a hurricane hits land it runs out of warm, moist air and its winds weaken; over cold water it loses its fuel too.
The IPCC (2021) finds a likely rise in the share of major hurricanes over four decades, and projects a larger share of the most intense storms with more warming.
The IPCC has low confidence in long-term trends in the total number of tropical cyclones.

title: A hurricane's cold wake
description: A hurricane churns up cooler water from below and leaves a cooler sea behind it.

facts.text: A hurricane's winds churn up cooler water from below, so the sea it leaves behind can be several degrees Celsius cooler.

title: The ocean as a heat store
description: Water absorbs lots of heat with little temperature change: the top few meters of ocean hold as much heat as the whole atmosphere.

facts.text: The top few meters of the ocean store as much heat as Earth's entire atmosphere.
Water can absorb large amounts of heat without a large rise in temperature, and it is slower to heat up and cool down than air or land.

title: The ocean takes up the extra heat
description: The ocean has absorbed about 91% of the extra heat in the climate system, and marine heatwaves have roughly doubled since the 1980s.

facts.text: The ocean has taken up about 91% of the extra heat trapped in the climate system; the atmosphere got about 1% (IPCC, 2021).
It is virtually certain the upper ocean (to 700 m) has warmed since the 1970s, and extremely likely that human influence is the main driver (IPCC, 2021).
Marine heatwaves, spells of persistent, unusually warm sea temperatures, have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s (IPCC, 2021, high confidence).

title: The ocean absorbs carbon dioxide
description: The ocean takes up about 30% of released CO2: it dissolves at the surface, best in cold water, and plankton carry some of it deep.

facts.text: The ocean absorbs about 30% of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere.
Carbon dioxide dissolves into seawater at the surface, and colder water can hold more of it than warmer water; once dissolved, it reacts to form carbonic acid.
Phytoplankton take up carbon dioxide as they photosynthesize; the carbon passes up the food web, and a portion sinks, staying deep for hundreds to thousands of years.

title: Ocean acidification
description: Absorbed CO2 lowers the ocean's pH, leaving fewer carbonate ions for shell builders; human emissions are the main driver.

facts.text: Ocean acidification is a long-term drop in the ocean's pH caused mainly by taking up carbon dioxide from the air.
It is virtually certain that human-caused carbon dioxide emissions are the main driver of today's acidification of the surface open ocean (IPCC, 2021).
Acidification leaves fewer carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells and skeletons, so oysters, clams, sea urchins and corals struggle to build them.

title: Why sea level rises
description: Seas rise because warming water expands and melting land ice adds water: about 21 to 24 cm since 1880.

facts.text: Global average sea level has risen about 21 to 24 cm since 1880.
Sea level rises for two main reasons: seawater expands as it warms, and melting glaciers and ice sheets on land add water to the ocean.
From 1971 to 2018, warming expansion caused about 50% of sea-level rise, melting glaciers about 22% and ice sheets about 20% (IPCC, 2021).

title: How fast the seas rise
description: The rate of rise has roughly tripled since the early 1900s, and the IPCC projects further rise this century that depends on emissions.

facts.text: Global sea level rose about 1.3 mm a year from 1901 to 1971 and about 3.7 mm a year from 2006 to 2018; human influence was very likely the main driver of these increases since at least 1971 (IPCC).
By 2100, the IPCC's likely rise is 0.28–0.55 m with very low emissions and 0.63–1.01 m with very high emissions, compared with 1995–2014.
Rises approaching 2 m by 2100 cannot be ruled out because ice-sheet behavior is deeply uncertain, and sea level is committed to keep rising for centuries (IPCC).

title: Garbage patches gather in gyres
description: Gyres draw floating debris into their calm centers; the best-known patch lies between Hawaii and California.

facts.text: Garbage patches are large areas of ocean where litter, fishing gear and other debris collect, formed by rotating currents called gyres.
A gyre's circling currents draw floating debris into its calm, stable center.
The best-known garbage patch lies in the North Pacific gyre, between Hawaii and California.
Captain Charles Moore came upon the Pacific patch in 1997, sailing from Hawaii to California after a yacht race, and saw plastic all around his boat.

title: What garbage patches are made of
description: Garbage patches are mostly microplastics under 5 mm, spread like pepper in soup rather than an island of trash.

facts.text: Garbage patches are mostly microplastics, plastic pieces smaller than 5 mm, along with larger debris such as abandoned fishing nets.
A garbage patch is not an island of trash: NOAA likens it to pepper flakes swirling in a soup, spread from the surface to the ocean floor, and satellite images don't show it.
Because the debris is spread out and always moving, patches have no exact size and may never be fully cleaned up; NOAA says prevention is key, like turning off an overflowing tap.

title: Currents even out Earth's heat
description: Ocean currents move warm water from the equator and cold water from the poles, spreading heat around the planet.

facts.text: Ocean currents carry warm water away from the equator and cold water from the poles around the Earth, evening out the planet's heat.

title: Plankton: the ocean's drifters
description: Plankton are organisms that drift with tides and currents they cannot swim against; most are microscopic, but some jellyfish count too.

facts.text: Plankton, from the Greek for drifter, are organisms carried by tides and currents that cannot swim well enough to move against them; most are microscopic, but some jellyfish count too.

title: Phytoplankton: the base of the ocean food web
description: Phytoplankton catch sunlight near the surface and feed zooplankton, which feed larger animals; the tiniest of them make a big share of Earth's oxygen.

facts.text: Prochlorococcus, the smallest photosynthetic organism on Earth, produces up to 20% of the oxygen in our entire biosphere, more than all tropical rainforests on land combined.
Plankton divide into phytoplankton (plants) and zooplankton (animals, including jellyfish); most zooplankton eat phytoplankton, and most are in turn eaten by larger animals.

Like land plants, phytoplankton use chlorophyll to capture sunlight for photosynthesis; NASA calls them the foundation of the aquatic food web, feeding everything from zooplankton to multi-ton whales.
Phytoplankton blooms in the ocean may cover hundreds of square kilometers and are easily visible in satellite images.

title: Kelp forests
description: Kelp are fast-growing brown algae anchored by holdfasts and buoyed toward the light, forming shallow coastal forests full of life.

facts.text: Kelp are large brown algae, not plants, that grow in cool, nutrient-rich coastal waters; kelp forests line much of the west coast of North America.
Kelp anchor to rocky sea floors with root-like holdfasts and reach toward sunlight on flexible stipes and leaf-like blades; many have gas-filled bladders that hold the blades up.
Giant kelp, the largest marine alga, is one of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth: it can grow up to 2 feet (about 60 cm) in a single day.
Because kelp depends on light for photosynthesis, kelp forests form in shallow water and are rarely found deeper than about 15 to 40 m (49 to 131 feet).

Kelp forests give food and shelter to thousands of species of fish, invertebrates and marine mammals and hold more variety of life than almost any other ocean community; the floating canopy shades the water below.

title: Otters, urchins and kelp
description: Predators like sea otters keep kelp-grazing urchins in check; unchecked urchins can leave urchin barrens.

facts.text: Predators such as sea otters and sea stars keep sea urchins in balance; when urchin numbers surge, they can strip away entire kelp forests, leaving rocky urchin barrens.

title: Why reefs hold so much life
description: Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean but hold nearly a quarter of its species, because the structure polyps build offers food, shelter and nurseries.

facts.text: Coral reefs occur in less than 1% of the ocean, yet are home to nearly a quarter of all ocean species.
Most structures we call coral are made of hundreds to thousands of tiny animals called polyps, each of which secretes a hard outer skeleton of limestone.
Coral reefs give thousands of creatures, including fish, crabs and sea turtles, places to feed, shelter and raise their young; NOAA calls them the rainforests of the sea.

title: The coral and algae partnership
description: Algae in coral tissues pass most of the food they make to the coral, so reef builders need clear, warm, sunlit water.

facts.text: As much as 90% of the food the algae in a coral's tissues make by photosynthesis passes to the coral; the coral gives the algae shelter plus the carbon dioxide and water they need.
Shallow reef-building corals thrive in clear, warm, moving water in tropical and subtropical seas, where sunlight can reach the algae living in their tissues.

title: Why fish school
description: Schools help fish evade predators, find food and mates, and save energy.

facts.text: Fish swim together in schools to evade predators, find good feeding areas, find mates and save energy.
In a 2024 study led by Harvard zoologist Yangfan Zhang, giant danios schooling in groups of eight in turbulent water used up to 79% less energy than fish swimming alone.

title: How a school moves as one
description: With no leader, schooling fish follow their neighbors by sight and the lateral line, and alarms spread through the school in under a second.

facts.text: Schooling fish keep formation using vision and the lateral line, a line of cells along the body that feels pressure changes from neighbors' movements; in dark water they can coordinate only with their closest neighbors.
A fish school has no single leader: each fish times its tail beats to follow its neighbor, like dancers moving to the same beat.
When a predator strikes, only a few fish in a school may see or feel it, but the alarm spreads, and in less than a second thousands of fish can move as one shape.

title: Sea turtles come home
description: Hatchlings race to sea and grow up in sargassum; years later females return to nest on their home beach, likely guided by its magnetic signature.

facts.text: Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from the nest virtually all at once, which helps them overwhelm waiting predators, and find the sea by the beach's downward slope and the moon and stars reflected on the water.
Hatchlings that survive swim out to floating mats of sargassum seaweed offshore, where they spend their early years hiding and growing.
Years later, female sea turtles return to nest on the beaches where they themselves hatched.
Scientists think sea turtles find their home beach with Earth's magnetic field: each stretch of coast has its own magnetic signature, which hatchlings imprint on and use as adults to return.

title: The leatherback's Pacific crossing
description: Western Pacific leatherbacks, the largest turtles, cross the Pacific between Indonesian nesting beaches and North American feeding grounds on a diet of jellyfish.

facts.text: Western Pacific leatherbacks nest in Indonesia and feed off the Pacific coast of North America: a crossing of nearly 7,000 miles (about 11,000 km) that takes 10 to 12 months.
The leatherback is the largest turtle in the world, and it feeds on soft-bodied open-ocean prey such as jellyfish.

title: Dolphins hunt with sound
description: Sound travels fast and far in seawater, and dolphins read echoes to sense what they cannot see.

facts.text: Sound travels about 1,500 m per second in seawater, over four times faster than about 340 m per second in air, and it travels much farther in the sea.

Dolphins use echolocation to fill in what they cannot see: they send out sounds and read the echoes, focusing them with the melon on their forehead, and can interpret signals from half a mile (about 800 m) away.

title: Dolphin names and teamwork
description: Bottlenose dolphins have name-like signature whistles and hunt together by herding schools of fish.

facts.text: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a distinctive call that works like a name and tells others who it is.
Bottlenose dolphins work together to herd fish into tight groups, then take turns charging through the school to feed; they may also trap schools against sandbars and seawalls.

title: Pinnipeds: flipper-footed mammals
description: Seals, sea lions and walruses are pinnipeds, mammals that live in the ocean but come ashore for long periods.

facts.text: Pinniped means fin- or flipper-footed; the group includes seals, sea lions and walruses, marine mammals that live in the ocean but can come on land for long periods.

title: Seal or sea lion?
description: Sea lions have ear flaps, walk on rotated rear flippers, paddle with front flippers and bark; seals have ear holes, crawl on their bellies, swim with rear flippers and are quiet.

facts.text: Sea lions are more likely than seals to perform in aquariums and marine shows.
Sea lions have small external ear flaps, earning them the nickname eared seals; true seals have ear holes but no flaps.
On land, sea lions "walk" by rotating their rear flippers under their bodies; seals cannot, so they move on their bellies in a caterpillar-like motion.
Seals swim by moving their rear flippers back and forth, like a fish's tail; sea lions paddle with their long front flippers.
Sea lions are noisy, known for a loud bark; seals are quiet and vocalize with soft grunts, growls or hisses.
Seals are better adapted to life in the water than on land and are more streamlined swimmers than sea lions, which are more agile on land.

title: Albatrosses: gliders of the open sea
description: Albatrosses glide for hours on the wind, spend years at sea and come ashore only to breed; Wisdom is the oldest known wild bird.

facts.text: Wisdom, a Laysan albatross first banded on Midway Atoll in 1956, is the world's oldest known wild bird and was still laying eggs in her 70s.
The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, more than 340 cm (11 feet).
Albatrosses can stay aloft in windy weather for hours without flapping: they glide downwind toward the sea, then turn into the wind to lift back up.
Albatrosses come ashore only to breed, usually on remote ocean islands, and a young albatross can spend 5 to 10 years at sea before coming to land to mate.

title: Puffins fly underwater
description: Puffins use their wings as paddles to dive for small fish, which they carry crosswise in the bill.

facts.text: Atlantic puffins "fly" underwater, using their wings as paddles and their webbed feet to steer, and can dive to about 200 feet (about 60 m).
A puffin can catch as many as 10 small fish in a row and carry them crosswise in its bill back to the nest.

title: How seabirds drink seawater
description: Salt glands above seabirds' eyes remove the extra salt from seawater.

facts.text: Seabirds have a pair of salt glands above their eyes that act like an extra set of kidneys, pulling surplus salt from the blood; it drips out of the nostrils as brine, and all seabirds can desalinate seawater this way.

title: Why seas need sharks
description: Sharks keep prey populations in balance and, by their presence alone, can protect habitats such as seagrass beds.

facts.text: As apex predators, sharks help keep ocean ecosystems in balance by preying on sick, weak or overabundant animals, which indirectly helps protect habitats like coral reefs; when sharks decline, the ripple effects can be dramatic.

In Shark Bay, Western Australia, tiger sharks change when, where and how dugongs and green turtles graze seagrass; the grazers crowd to safer bank edges, and the seagrass beds might be very different without sharks.

title: The decline of oceanic sharks
description: Oceanic sharks and rays have fallen by 71% since 1970, driven by fishing.

facts.text: A 2021 study in Nature found that since 1970 the global abundance of oceanic sharks and rays has fallen by 71%, driven by an 18-fold rise in relative fishing pressure.

title: The thin sunlit layer
description: The ocean's sunlight-powered food makers work in roughly the top 5% of an average water column, and nearly all the life in this chapter depends on them.

facts.text: With too little light for photosynthesis below about 200 m and an average ocean depth of about 3,700 m, sunlight-powered food making happens in roughly the top 5% of an average water column.

title: The ocean's depth zones
description: By light: sunlight zone to 200 m, twilight zone to 1,000 m, then the midnight zone, the abyss and the hadal zone in trenches.

facts.text: The top 200 m of the ocean is the sunlight zone; from 200 to 1,000 m lies the twilight zone, where light fades rapidly with depth.
Below 1,000 m lie the midnight zone (1,000 to 4,000 m), the abyss (4,000 to 6,000 m) and the hadal zone (6,000 m and deeper).
The hadal zone is found only in ocean trenches, and it is named after Hades, the Greek god of the underworld.
Below 1,000 m, the only light is made by living things.

title: The midnight zone
description: From 1,000 to 4,000 m, dark and a steady 4°C, the midnight zone holds about 70% of all seawater: the largest single habitat on Earth.

facts.text: The midnight zone stays at a steady 4°C and holds about 70% of all seawater, making it the largest single habitat on Earth.

title: The nightly migration
description: Every night, twilight-zone animals swim up to feed and sink again at dawn, the largest animal migration on Earth, probably to hide from predators that hunt by silhouette.

facts.text: During World War II, US Navy sonar showed what looked like a sea floor that sat deep by day and rose near the surface after dark; it was a layer of migrating animals.

As darkness falls, many twilight-zone fish, squid, plankton and other animals swim up to feed near the surface, then return to deeper water at daybreak: the largest animal migration on Earth, every 24 hours.
Rising only at night may help twilight-zone animals avoid predators, which hunt by spotting the outline of prey against the faint light above.

title: A crowded twilight zone
description: The twilight zone may hold more fish by weight than the rest of the ocean, and its bristlemouths may be the most abundant vertebrates on Earth.

facts.text: Scientists estimate the twilight zone may hold more fish, by weight, than all the rest of the ocean combined.
The bristlemouth, a small twilight-zone fish, is thought to be the most abundant vertebrate on Earth, possibly numbering in the quadrillions.

title: Bioluminescence
description: Many ocean animals make light by a chemical reaction. It is common in the open ocean, rare on land, and usually blue because blue travels best in seawater.

facts.text: Bioluminescence is light made by a living thing through a chemical reaction between an enzyme and another substance; different species use different chemicals, so it probably evolved many separate times.
In a 2017 MBARI study of Monterey Bay, from the surface down to 4,000 m, three quarters of the animals could make their own light.
Bioluminescence is relatively rare on land but very common in the open ocean.
Most bioluminescence in the ocean is blue, because blue is the light that travels best through seawater.

title: What living light is for
description: Deep animals use light to escape (glowing clouds), to hide (belly lights that erase a silhouette) and to hunt.

facts.text: Some deep-sea shrimp release a cloud of glowing fluid from glands near the mouth, which probably confuses or distracts an attacker.
Some twilight-zone fish have rows of light organs on their bellies that match the dim light from above, hiding their silhouette from predators looking up.

title: The giant squid
description: The giant squid reaches about 13 m, with eyes up to 27 cm that may spot sperm whales; it was first photographed alive in the wild in 2004 by following sperm whales.

facts.text: In 2004, Japanese researchers Tsunemi Kubodera and Kyoichi Mori took the first images of a live giant squid in the wild, attacking bait at about 900 m off the Ogasawara Islands; they chose the spot by following sperm whales, which hunt giant squid.
The giant squid can reach roughly 13 m long, and its eyes, up to 27 cm across, are among the largest of any living animal.
A giant squid's huge eyes may let it make out the shape of a hunting sperm whale more than 120 m away.

title: The colossal squid
description: The heaviest invertebrate, up to about 500 kg, known for a century mostly from stomachs, was first filmed alive in its habitat in 2025: a 30 cm juvenile.

facts.text: The colossal squid, which lives in the cold, deep Southern Ocean, can weigh about 500 kg, making it the heaviest invertebrate on Earth.
For 100 years after it was named, the colossal squid was met mainly as remains in the stomachs of whales and seabirds.
On March 9, 2025, a team on Schmidt Ocean Institute's ship Falkor (too) filmed a live colossal squid in its habitat for the first time: a 30 cm juvenile at 600 m near the South Sandwich Islands.

title: How the anglerfish hunts
description: Instead of spending energy searching, the anglerfish waits with a glowing lure and a big mouth of backward-pointing teeth.

facts.text: In November 2014, MBARI filmed a black seadevil anglerfish alive about 580 m down in Monterey Canyon, the first video of the species in its habitat; anglerfish are among the most rarely seen deep-sea fishes.

Where food is scarce, deep-sea anglerfish save energy by luring prey instead of swimming around searching, which costs a lot of energy; the lure of most adult females glows with bacteria living inside it.
Deep-sea anglerfish have large mouths with sharp, backward-pointing teeth, and some have been known to swallow prey larger than themselves.

title: Anglerfish partners for life
description: In some deep-sea anglerfish families, the tiny male fuses to the much larger female for life, sharing her bloodstream.

facts.text: In some deep-sea anglerfish families, the tiny male bites onto a much larger female and stays for life: his mouth fuses with her skin and their bloodstreams join.

title: Whale falls
description: A sunken whale feeds the deep in stages: scavengers strip the flesh, bone specialists move in, then bacteria in the bones power a community for decades.

facts.text: Much of the deep sea is fed by marine snow: a slow drizzle of dead plankton, waste and other particles sinking from above.
One whale fall can deliver as much food to the deep sea floor as thousands of years of marine snow.
Within days of a dead whale reaching the deep floor, scavengers such as sleeper sharks, hagfish, rattails and amphipods arrive, and they often strip it to the bone within months.

After a year or two, bacteria feed on fats and oils deep in the bones and release hydrogen sulfide, which supports a community built on chemosynthetic bacteria instead of sunlight; it can last for decades.

title: Bone-eating worms
description: Osedax worms, found on a whale in Monterey Canyon, have no mouth or stomach; roots and bacteria digest the fats and oils in whale bones.

facts.text: On a dead whale nearly 2,900 m down in Monterey Canyon, found in 2002, MBARI scientists discovered bone-eating worms; in 2004 they were named Osedax, Latin for "bone devourer."
Osedax worms have no mouth or stomach; green roots reach into the bone, where bacteria help digest the fats and oils inside.

title: Chemosynthesis at vents
description: At hydrothermal vents, microbes make food from hydrogen sulfide instead of sunlight, and whole animal communities live on it.

facts.text: In 1977, scientists exploring a spreading ridge near the Galapagos Islands found hydrothermal vents on the sea floor, with animals living around them.
Vent food webs run on chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis: microbes turn hydrogen sulfide from the vent fluid into food, which sustains tubeworms, shrimp and mussels.

title: The giant tubeworm's partners
description: Giant tubeworms have no mouth or gut; microbes living inside them make food from vent chemicals and share it.

facts.text: Giant tubeworms at vents stand up to about six feet (nearly 2 m) tall yet have no mouth or gut; microbes living inside them turn vent chemicals into food they share with the worm.

title: Deep-sea gigantism
description: Many deep animals outgrow their shallow relatives, perhaps because cold slows their lives, predators are few and big bodies cope better with scarce food.

facts.text: Giant isopods, deep-sea relatives of garden pill bugs, can grow more than 30 cm long.
Many deep-sea animals, such as giant isopods and the colossal squid, grow much larger than their shallow-water relatives, a pattern called deep-sea gigantism.
Cold deep water slows animals' metabolisms, and many deep-sea creatures grow and mature very slowly, which may help them reach large sizes.
Having few predators may also let deep-sea animals such as giant isopods grow large.
Where food is scarce, bigger bodies help: larger animals can travel farther to find food, use energy more efficiently and store more of it.
A giant isopod kept at an aquarium in Japan reportedly survived about five years without eating.

title: How little of the deep we have seen
description: People have visually observed less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor, which covers about 66% of Earth's surface.

facts.text: A 2025 study of about 44,000 deep-sea dives since 1958 found that people have visually observed less than 0.001% of the deep seafloor, an area about the size of Rhode Island.
The deep ocean, deeper than 200 m, covers about 66% of Earth's surface.
Judging all life on land from the same share, 0.001%, would mean studying an area about the size of Houston, Texas.

title: Species still unnamed
description: About a quarter of a million marine species are named, with millions more expected; in one deep Pacific plain about 90% of species had no name.

facts.text: Only about a quarter of a million marine species have been documented (the Ocean Census cites about 240,000), and millions more are thought to await discovery.
In a 2023 study of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a deep Pacific plain between Hawaii and Mexico about 5,000 m down, around 90% of the species recorded had no scientific name.

title: Surviving the deep
description: Deep animals cope with pressure by being mostly water with no air spaces; the deepest fish ever filmed swam at 8,336 m.

facts.text: In 2022, a University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology team filmed a juvenile snailfish at 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench off Japan, the deepest fish ever filmed.
Most deep-sea animals are largely water, which barely compresses, and without gas-filled spaces such as lungs or swim bladders they are far less affected by pressure.
Some ocean animals migrate 1,000 m up and down each day, passing through a 100-atmosphere range of pressure with no harm.
Red light never reaches the deep ocean, so red animals there look black and are hard to see; red and black animals predominate in the deep.

title: Beach sand from worn-down rock
description: Most beach sand is rock broken down by weathering and erosion and carried to the coast by rivers; hard, insoluble quartz survives best, so tan beaches are mostly quartz and feldspar.

facts.text: Sand forms when rocks break down by weathering and erosion over thousands to millions of years; streams and rivers carry the pieces toward the sea, breaking them down further.
Quartz is by far the commonest mineral in sand: it is hard, does not split easily and barely dissolves, so it outlasts other minerals.
The tan color of most sand beaches comes from quartz tinted light brown by iron oxide, plus feldspar.

title: Sand colors from local sources
description: A beach's color reveals its local sources: black sand from lava that shatters in the sea, pink sand from foraminifera shells, and white tropical sand ground from coral by parrotfish.

facts.text: Black sand forms when lava enters the sea: its surface quickly cools and shatters into fragments, making Hawaii's famous black sand.
Bermuda's pink beaches get their color from the crushed shells of foraminifera, single-celled sea creatures.

Parrotfish scrape algae off rock and dead coral, grind the coral in their guts and excrete it as white sand, hundreds of pounds a year from one fish; up to 70% of white-beach sand in Hawaii and the Caribbean may be theirs.

title: How waves wear back cliffs
description: Waves quarry cracked rock with trapped, compressed air and water impact, and abrade it with sand and stones; a notch cut at the cliff base makes the rock above fall, so cliffs retreat and leave wave-cut platforms.

facts.text: Breaking waves trap and compress air against the shore; together with the impact of the water, this can pry loose fractured rock, a process called quarrying.
Breaking waves also throw sand and stones against the shore, wearing it down by abrasion.

Waves erode a notch at the base of a sea cliff; the overhanging rock falls, the cliff retreats, and a gently sloping rock ledge called a wave-cut platform is left from the cliff's foot to below low tide.

title: Sea caves start at weak spots
description: Waves widen weaknesses such as faults, fractures and soft layers first, so most sea caves form along them; long erosion can turn caves into arches and arches into stacks.

facts.text: Most sea caves form along weaknesses in the rock, such as faults, fractures or layers of softer rock, which waves and the sediment they carry enlarge first.
Most caves on California's Channel Islands are sea caves formed by waves eroding along narrow fractures in the rock.
Painted Cave on Santa Cruz Island, in Channel Islands National Park, is about 370 m (1,227 ft) long, the largest sea cave in California.
With continued erosion of a headland, caves can become sea arches, and a collapsed arch leaves a sea stack.

title: Estuaries: where rivers meet the sea
description: An estuary is where river water mixes with seawater into brackish water whose saltiness keeps changing; estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems and are nurseries for young sea life.

facts.text: Estuaries are usually found where rivers meet the sea; their water is brackish, a mix of fresh water draining from the land and salty seawater.
When low tide leaves oysters in water that is too fresh, they close their shells and stop feeding until saltier water returns.
Estuaries are among the most productive ecosystems in the world; they filter runoff and are nursery grounds for many species, including many fish people catch, earning the name nurseries of the sea.
The Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the United States, is the drowned valley of the Susquehanna River, flooded as sea level rose after the last ice age.

title: Mangroves: trees in salt water
description: Mangroves grow where tides flood tropical and subtropical coasts, handle salt by filtering it at their roots or shedding it through leaf glands, and their roots trap sediment, shelter fish and protect shores.

facts.text: Mangroves are trees of the coastal intertidal zone, most flooded at least twice a day, with tangled prop roots like stilts; they grow only at tropical and subtropical latitudes because they cannot survive freezing.
Some mangroves filter salt out at their roots; others push it out through glands on their leaves, leaving salt crystals on top.
Mangrove roots slow tidal water so sediment settles out, shelter fish and other animals, and stabilize the coast, reducing erosion from storm surges, currents, waves and tides.

title: Hawaii's hot spot conveyor belt
description: The Hawaiian Islands formed over a hot spot as the Pacific Plate carried each volcano northwest, so the islands age in order; the next volcano, Kamaehuakanaloa, is still below the sea.

facts.text: The Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific Plate moved over a hot spot that feeds volcanoes; the plate carries each volcano away, so the islands get older toward the northwest.
The oldest exposed rocks on the Island of Hawaii, still over the hot spot, are less than 0.7 million years old; Kauai's oldest rocks are about 5.5 million years old and deeply eroded.

Kamaehuakanaloa (formerly Loihi), an active undersea volcano off the Island of Hawaii, rises to about 975 m below sea level; it is in the earliest stage, with small eruptions below the sea, and will take millennia to emerge.

title: Why old islands sink and shrink
description: Once off the hot spot, Hawaiian islands sink because their weight bends Earth's rigid outer layer, and rain, wind and waves wear them down, until the old end of the chain is only reefs and shoals.

facts.text: Hawaiian islands sink as they get older, mainly because their great weight bends the almost rigid outer layer of the Earth beneath them.
Older Hawaiian islands are worn down by erosion from the sea, rain and wind, so islands farther west are more eroded.
The Island of Hawaii sits at the young end of a chain of more than 125 volcanoes; Midway, far to the northwest, is about 28 million years old.
Through sinking and erosion, the old northwestern Hawaiian islands have dwindled to small patches of land, shoals and reefs, and the chain continues as submerged platforms.

title: How a ring-shaped atoll forms
description: A fringing reef around a volcanic island keeps growing upward as the island sinks, becoming a barrier reef and then an atoll; where cool water slows coral too much, as past Kure Atoll, reefs drown.

facts.text: A fringing reef grows from a volcanic island's shore; as the island sinks, the reef becomes a barrier reef separated from land by a lagoon, and when the island sinks below sea level a ring of reef around a lagoon, an atoll, remains.
An atoll forms because the reef keeps growing upward while the volcanic island sinks; barrier reefs and atolls can take from 100,000 to 30 million years to fully form.

Kure Atoll, the northernmost coral atoll, sits where cooler water slows coral growth until it only just matches the island's sinking; past it, reefs cannot keep up and drown. This limit is called the Darwin Point.

title: Darwin's atoll idea and its proof
description: Darwin reasoned out atoll formation during the Beagle voyage before seeing a true coral reef and published in 1842; drilling at Enewetak in 1952 found volcanic rock beneath more than 1 km of coral.

facts.text: Charles Darwin worked out his theory of coral atolls on the west coast of South America, during the Beagle voyage, before he had seen a true coral reef, while thinking about land slowly rising and sinking; he published it in 1842.
In 1952, in the first geologic drilling of an atoll, drills at Enewetak went through more than 1 km of coral before reaching volcanic rock (Britannica: about 1,400 m below the reef top).

title: What makes a good harbor
description: A harbor shelters ships from wind, waves and currents and is deep enough with room to turn; most are natural, such as bays, estuaries and rias, river valleys drowned by rising seas like Sydney Harbour.

facts.text: A harbor is water sheltered from wind, waves and currents, so ships can anchor safely and load or unload cargo and passengers.
A harbor must be deep enough to keep ships from touching bottom, with room for them to turn and pass each other.
Most harbors are natural, found in bays, coves, fjords, lagoons and estuaries that already give shelter.
A ria is a funnel-shaped inlet formed when sea level rose after the ice-age glaciers melted and flooded the lower part of a river valley.
Sydney Harbour (Port Jackson) is a drowned river valley estuary and one of the world's finest natural harbors.

title: Building a harbor where there is none
