description: Where nature gives no shelter, breakwaters block waves and dredging keeps water deep; the Allies' Mulberry harbors of 1944 show both the idea and its weak point when a storm destroyed one.

facts.text: Breakwaters, huge walls of concrete, steel and wire, are the most important part of an artificial harbor, absorbing or deflecting waves; dredging removes sand and sediment to keep harbors deep.
German forces had fortified the Channel ports, so for D-Day (June 6, 1944) the Allies built two artificial Mulberry harbors in Britain and floated them to Normandy.

The Mulberries' breakwaters were sunken concrete caissons and scuttled ships; a storm from June 19, 1944 destroyed the American harbor by June 22, while the British one at Arromanches served for 10 months.

title: How mollusks build shells
description: A mollusk's mantle secretes its shell, mostly calcium carbonate made from calcium and carbonate in seawater, often in three layers with a smooth inner layer that in some mollusks is nacre.

facts.text: A mollusk's shell is made by its mantle, tissue that secretes proteins and minerals; the shell is mostly calcium carbonate, with no more than about 2% protein.
Shellfish build their calcium carbonate shells from calcium and carbonate ions in seawater.
Many shells have three layers: an outer protein layer, a calcified prismatic layer and a smooth inner layer, which in some mollusks is nacre, or mother-of-pearl.

title: Shells grow at the edge and keep a record
description: A mollusk never sheds its shell but adds material at the edges; ocean quahogs add a band a year, which let scientists count Ming the clam's 507 years.

facts.text: Mollusks don't shed their shells, so shells enlarge as the animal grows by adding new material at their edges.
Ming, an ocean quahog clam dredged off Iceland in 2006, was 507 years old, the oldest individual animal known, counted from the band its shell adds each year; its first bands date to about 1499.

title: How a mollusk makes a pearl
description: An irritant stuck in a mollusk's tissue gets coated, layer upon layer, with shell material; only mollusks that use nacre make the shimmering, strong gem pearls.

facts.text: Natural pearls form when a tiny irritant, such as a parasite or bit of debris, gets stuck in a mollusk's tissue and cannot be flushed out; the mollusk coats it with shell material, layer upon layer.

Oysters, mussels and clams can all make pearls, but only certain mollusks coat them in nacre: organic secretions plus aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate, stacked like bricks and mortar, which is very strong and gives gem pearls their sheen.

title: Cultured pearls
description: Cultured pearls are started on purpose: a shell bead and a piece of mantle tissue go into a host mollusk, the tissue coats the bead with nacre over two to five years; Mikimoto pioneered the method in the 1890s.

facts.text: Natural pearls form without human help; for a cultured pearl, a technician inserts a shell bead and a small piece of mantle tissue into a host mollusk, the tissue forms a sac and coats the bead with nacre, taking two to five years.
In the early 1890s in Japan, Mikimoto Kokichi got pearl oysters to form half pearls around beads he had inserted.

title: Why coasts wear away
description: Storms and waves move beach sand along and off the coast, and coasts cut off from sediment retreat inland; rising seas, projected in 2022 to add 25 to 30 cm on US coasts by 2050, will speed erosion.

facts.text: When the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was completed in 1870 it stood about 460 m (1,500 ft) from the ocean; by 1970 erosion had left it about 37 m (120 ft) from the water's edge.
After groins and beach nourishment were tried, the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse was moved about 880 m (2,900 ft) inland between June 17 and July 9, 1999.
Breaking waves move sand along the coast, eroding it in one place and depositing it in another, and storms are the primary cause of beach erosion along many coasts.
Coasts need fresh sediment from rivers and other sources; sediment-starved coasts erode and migrate inland.

A February 2022 report by NOAA, NASA and other US agencies projected that sea level along US coasts will rise 25 to 30 cm (10 to 12 inches) on average by 2050, about as much as in the previous 100 years.
USGS studies project that beaches and coastal cliffs will erode faster as sea level rises.

title: Defending a coast, and the trade-offs
description: Groins trap sand on one side and starve the beach beyond; seawalls protect land but the beach in front can vanish; adding sand is costly and temporary; living shorelines use natural materials.

facts.text: Groins, walls built out across the beach, trap sand on their updrift side, while the beach on the downdrift side loses sand to the continuing longshore movement.
A seawall protects the land behind it, but the beach in front can disappear, leaving waves to strike the wall head-on; hardened shorelines often increase erosion.
Adding sand to a beach (beach nourishment) is expensive and not a permanent solution; living shorelines stabilize coasts with natural materials such as plants, sand, rock or oyster shells.

title: Surtsey: an island's life in fast-forward
description: Surtsey rose off Iceland in 1963 to 1967; waves have since cut away about half of it, carving cliffs in cracked lava, while its hard palagonite tuff core is expected to outlast the rest.

facts.text: Surtsey, off Iceland's south coast, formed in an eruption that broke the sea surface in November 1963 and lasted until June 1967.
Surtsey measured about 2.7 km2 when the eruption ended; by 2002, 35 years later, wave erosion had cut it to about 1.4 km2, about half.
On Surtsey's southwest, where the lava was badly cracked, waves broke down a strip of land up to 650 m wide and cut sea cliffs up to 75 m high.
Elsewhere on Surtsey, lava has protected the loose volcanic ash (tephra) behind it from the waves.

Surtsey's core of palagonite tuff, volcanic ash hardened into rock, resists wave erosion far better than loose ash or lava; researchers expect that after about 160 years only this core will be left, ringed by steep cliffs.

title: The Arctic Ocean: small, shallow and ringed by land
description: The Arctic is the smallest and shallowest ocean, about 1.5 times the size of the US, almost encircled by North America, Eurasia and Greenland. Nansen showed its center is deep ocean.

facts.text: The Arctic Ocean is almost completely encircled by the landmasses of North America, Eurasia and Greenland.
The Arctic Ocean is the smallest of the five ocean basins, yet about 1.5 times as big as the United States, and ice covers almost all of it for most of the year.

In 1893 Fridtjof Nansen froze his specially built ship, the Fram, into the pack ice north of Siberia; the drifting ice carried it across the Arctic for about three years, and he found the Polar Basin is deep ocean.
The Arctic Ocean averages only about 987 m deep, the shallowest of the five oceans; that is roughly a quarter of the whole ocean's average of about 3,700 m.

title: The Arctic's fresh top layer
description: The Arctic holds about 1% of ocean water but gets about 11% of river discharge. Pacific and river water give it a cold, fresher, lighter top layer that floats and helps sea ice grow.

facts.text: The Arctic Ocean contains only about 1% of global ocean water yet receives about 11% of global river discharge (NOAA Arctic Report Card 2021).
Water from the Pacific and from rivers in Russia and Canada gives the Arctic Ocean a cold, fresher, less dense surface layer, which allows more sea ice to grow in the Arctic than in the Antarctic.

title: How sea ice forms and grows with the seasons
description: Polar seawater freezes at about −1.8 C, first as needle-like frazil, then grease or pancake ice. Sea ice grows in winter and melts in summer; the two poles peak six months apart.

facts.text: Fresh water freezes at 0 °C, but salt lowers the freezing point: polar seawater begins to freeze at about −1.8 °C.
Sea ice starts as small needle-like crystals called frazil; in calm water they form a smooth, oily-looking film called grease ice, and in rough water they gather into round, slushy pancake ice.
Arctic sea ice usually peaks in March and reaches its minimum in September; Antarctic sea ice usually peaks in September.
On average, only about a third of the Arctic's late-winter sea ice remains at the end of the summer melt.

title: Sea ice squeezes out its salt
description: Growing ice pushes salt out: some is trapped as brine, which drains over the years, and the rest makes the water below saltier and denser, so it sinks.

facts.text: As sea ice forms, it pushes salt out; some is trapped between the crystals in pockets of very salty liquid called brine, which is why new ice is salty.
As sea ice ages its brine drains out, so ice four or more years old is nearly free of brine.
The salt that forming sea ice pushes into the ocean makes the water saltier and denser, so it sinks.

title: Icebergs are land ice gone to sea
description: An iceberg is a piece of glacier or ice shelf that broke off (calved), so it is frozen fresh water from snow. Most North Atlantic icebergs come from west Greenland.

facts.text: An iceberg is ice that broke off a glacier or ice shelf and floats in open water; the breaking off is called calving.
Glaciers form from snow that piles up long enough to turn to ice, so icebergs are frozen fresh water, unlike sea ice, which freezes from seawater in the ocean.
Most icebergs that enter the North Atlantic shipping lanes come from the tidewater glaciers of west Greenland and take 1 to 3 years to drift there.

title: Why most of an iceberg is underwater
description: Freezing locks water molecules into a spread-out lattice, so ice is about 9% less dense than water. That is only a little lighter, so about 90% of an iceberg floats below the waterline.

facts.text: When water freezes its molecules lock into an orderly lattice that spreads them out, so ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water; that is why ice cubes float.
About 90% of an iceberg is below the waterline (the US Coast Guard puts it at about seven eighths).

title: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current
description: The largest wind-driven current on Earth flows west to east all the way around Antarctica, linking three oceans and walling the Southern Ocean off from waters to the north.

facts.text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the largest wind-driven current on Earth, flows west to east all the way around Antarctica; it is the only current that circles the planet, linking the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current acts as a barrier, separating the Southern Ocean from the waters to its north.

title: Fish built for freezing water
description: Antarctic icefish have no red blood cells or hemoglobin and survive with big hearts in oxygen-rich water; Antarctic notothenioid fish carry antifreeze proteins, found by DeVries in the late 1960s.

facts.text: Antarctic icefish lack red blood cells and hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein that makes blood red; most of the 16 icefish species live in the Antarctic.
Icefish have larger hearts and gill blood vessels, circulating a greater volume of blood to take enough oxygen from the oxygen-rich Antarctic water.
In the late 1960s Arthur DeVries discovered antifreeze proteins in Antarctic notothenioid fishes; they bind to ice crystals in the blood and keep the fish from freezing.

title: Krill: the Southern Ocean's link
description: Antarctic krill, shrimp-like crustaceans about 5 cm long, swarm in vast numbers, may have the largest biomass of any wild animal species, and feed most of the region's larger animals.

facts.text: Antarctic krill may have the largest total biomass of any wild animal species; the best estimate is about 379 million tonnes.
Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) are small, translucent, shrimp-like crustaceans about 5 cm long that live in vast, dense swarms.

Krill graze on microscopic algae (phytoplankton) and are the main food for many of the Southern Ocean's larger animals, including penguins, whales and fish, linking the producers to the top predators.
The blue whale, the largest animal known to have lived, feeds almost only on krill and may eat up to 6 tons of it a day.

title: Sea ice: the krill nursery
description: Young krill spend the winter under sea ice, whose complex underside gives shelter from predators and access to food, so winter sea ice is their nursery and feeding ground.

facts.text: Young krill overwinter under the sea ice, where the complex underside of the ice gives them shelter from predators and access to food; winter sea ice is their nursery and feeding habitat.

title: Whales that commute to the poles
description: Humpbacks feed on krill and small fish in cold polar waters in summer, then swim as far as about 8,000 km to tropical breeding grounds, living on stored blubber through the winter.

facts.text: Humpback whales feed in summer in cold, productive high-latitude waters, straining krill and small fish through their baleen, and build fat (blubber) that sustains them through the winter.
Some humpback populations swim about 8,000 km (5,000 miles) between tropical breeding grounds, where they mate and calve in winter, and colder feeding grounds.
In the Arctic summer, migratory humpback, minke and fin whales arrive from southern wintering grounds and leave again as it cools.

title: The Arctic's year-round whales
description: Only belugas, narwhals and bowheads live in the Arctic all year. The narwhal tusk is a tooth; the bowhead breaks ice with its head, has the thickest blubber and may live 200 years.

facts.text: Only three whale species live in the Arctic year-round: the beluga, the narwhal and the bowhead.
The narwhal's tusk is actually an enlarged left tooth.
A bowhead whale's large, reinforced skull lets it break through sea ice about 20 cm (8 inches) thick.
The bowhead has the thickest blubber of any whale, about 43 to 48 cm (17 to 19 inches), and studies suggest it may live more than 200 years.

title: Keeping a breathing hole open
description: Seals under the ice must keep holes open to breathe. Antarctic Weddell seals rasp the ice with their teeth; Arctic ringed seals scrape with their claws through ice up to about 1.8 m thick.

facts.text: Weddell seals are the most southerly mammal living permanently in Antarctica, and they breathe through cracks and holes in the ice, even in the dark of winter.
When a Weddell seal's breathing hole freezes over, it rasps the ice open with its canine and incisor teeth, which can wear down until it can no longer feed or keep its holes open.
Arctic ringed seals use their sharp claws to make and keep open breathing holes through ice that may be about 1.8 m (6 feet) thick or more.

title: Sea ice as a seal's home
description: Ringed seals raise pups in snow-covered lairs on the ice and are polar bears' main prey; crabeater seals live their whole lives on Antarctic pack ice, straining krill with sieve-like teeth.

facts.text: Ringed seals, the smallest and most common Arctic seal, give birth to and nurse their pups on the ice in snow-covered lairs.
Polar bears spend much of their time on the sea ice hunting ringed seals, their primary prey.
Crabeater seals eat krill, not crabs: their specially adapted teeth have extra projections that strain krill from gulped seawater.
Crabeater seals spend their whole lives in the pack ice around Antarctica, resting and breeding on it, and are the most abundant seal in the Southern Ocean.

title: Why the Titanic sank
description: On its maiden voyage the Titanic kept its speed despite ice warnings, struck an iceberg at 11:40 pm on April 14, 1912, flooded at least five compartments (it could survive four) and sank at 2:20 am.

facts.text: The Titanic left Southampton, England, for New York City on its maiden voyage on April 10, 1912.
The Titanic's hull was divided into watertight compartments and it could stay afloat with four flooded, so many claimed it was unsinkable.
On April 14, 1912, the Titanic received iceberg warnings through the day; its course was shifted slightly south, but its speed was not lowered.
The Titanic struck the iceberg at 11:40 PM on April 14, 1912, and water was soon reported in at least five of its compartments.
Scientists who studied the wreck found the iceberg left a series of thin gashes in the hull, as well as brittle fracturing.
At 2:20 AM on April 15, 1912, the Titanic's stern slipped under and the ship was gone.

title: Too few lifeboats, and a patrol for ice
description: The Titanic carried 20 lifeboats for 1,178 people with over 2,200 aboard, and more than 1,500 died. The 1914 SOLAS convention followed, creating the International Ice Patrol.

facts.text: The Titanic's 20 lifeboats had room for only 1,178 people, but more than 2,200 were aboard.
More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,224 people aboard the Titanic died.
The Titanic disaster led to the first Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) convention in 1914, which established the International Ice Patrol to monitor iceberg danger in the North Atlantic; it still does.

title: The shrinking Arctic sea ice
description: Satellites since 1979 show September Arctic ice shrinking about 12% per decade; the 20 lowest minimums came in 2007-2026. The IPCC finds human influence the main driver.

facts.text: NSIDC's September 2026 analysis found that the 20 years from 2007 to 2026 have the lowest 20 Arctic sea ice minimum extents in the satellite record.

Satellites have measured Arctic sea ice since 1979; September ice is shrinking about 12% per decade relative to 1981-2010 (NASA: 12.2%; NSIDC, September 2026: 11.8% for 1979-2026), and the record low came in 2012.

The IPCC (2021) found human influence very likely the main driver of the decrease in Arctic sea ice between 1979-1988 and 2010-2019, about 40% in September, and projects the Arctic is likely to be practically ice-free in September at least once before 2050 in all five scenarios.

title: Antarctic sea ice: a different story
description: The IPCC found no significant trend in Antarctic sea ice from 1979 to 2020, as regions changed in opposite ways; then the 2023 winter maximum set a record low by over a million square km.

facts.text: The IPCC (2021) found no significant trend in Antarctic sea ice area from 1979 to 2020, because of regionally opposing trends and large natural variability, and has low confidence in its projected decrease.
In 2023 Antarctic sea ice had its lowest winter maximum in the satellite record, more than one million square km below the previous record low.

title: Why losing sea ice matters
description: Ice reflects 50 to 70% of sunlight but open ocean only 6%, so melting lets the sea absorb more heat and melt more ice. Ringed seals and krill depend on the ice.

facts.text: Sea ice reflects 50 to 70% of incoming sunlight, while open ocean reflects only about 6% and absorbs the rest, so losing ice lets the ocean warm and more ice melt.
Loss of sea ice and of the snow cover on it is the main threat to ringed seals.
Scientists warn that sea-ice decline, together with ocean warming and acidification, could affect how many krill there are and where they live.

title: Polar opposites: why the south's ice is younger
description: The Arctic is an ocean ringed by land and the Antarctic a continent ringed by ocean. Landlocked Arctic ice has lasted years; Antarctic ice drifts north and melts, so most is under a year old.

facts.text: The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by continents, while the Antarctic is a continent surrounded by ocean.

Multiyear ice, 2 to 4 m thick, has been more common in the landlocked Arctic; around Antarctica no land stops the ice drifting north until it melts, so most is under a year old, usually 1 to 2 m thick.

title: Settling the Pacific by canoe
description: People crossed the open Pacific long before Europeans: Lapita voyagers reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 3,000 years ago, and Polynesians settled Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa by about 1300 CE.

facts.text: By the time European explorers entered the Pacific Ocean in the 16th century (the 1500s), almost all its habitable islands had been settled for hundreds of years.
People inhabited Australia and New Guinea by 50,000 years ago, reaching them across short stretches of sea.
Lapita, a culture named after a site in New Caledonia and known by its distinctive pottery, spread from New Guinea east as far as Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 3,000 years ago.
Polynesian culture developed at the eastern edge of the Lapita region, in Tonga and Samoa.
High-precision radiocarbon dating (Wilmshurst and others, 2011) shows voyagers reached Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa New Zealand between about 1190 and 1290 CE, so by about 1300 CE.

title: Polynesian voyaging canoes
description: Double-hulled voyaging canoes, built with stone, bone and coral tools, carried crops and animals on planned voyages of more than 3,200 km.

facts.text: Polynesian voyaging canoes were two hulls lashed together with crossbeams and a deck between them, with sails woven from coconut or pandanus leaves.
Settlers carried plants such as taro, breadfruit, banana and coconut, and animals including the pig, dog and chicken, which suggests they planned to colonize the islands they had found.
Voyaging canoes made voyages of over 2,000 miles (more than 3,200 km) along Polynesia's longest sea roads, such as Hawaiʻi to Tahiti.

title: The Hawaiian star compass
description: Wayfinders memorize where stars rise and set; the Hawaiian star compass divides the horizon into 32 houses, a mental map of directions.

facts.text: Hawaiian navigator Nainoa Thompson says wayfinders, with no compass and no watch, use about 220 stars at night, memorizing where each one comes up and goes down.
The Hawaiian star compass, developed by Nainoa Thompson, is a mental construct, not an object: it divides the horizon into 32 houses where the Sun, stars, Moon and planets rise and set.
Nainoa Thompson learned wayfinding from Mau Piailug, a master navigator from the island of Satawal in Micronesia.

title: Latitude from stars, longitude from clocks
description: A star's height above the horizon gives latitude; longitude needs a clock keeping home time, since each hour of difference is 15 degrees. Harrison's H4 solved it at sea.

facts.text: Latitude can be found from the height of the Sun or the pole star; a sextant measures a star's angle above the horizon, which estimates the observer's latitude.
Sailing north toward Hawaiʻi, the Southern Cross sits lower each night; at Hawaiʻi's latitude the gap between its top and bottom stars equals the gap from the bottom star to the horizon.
Longitude has no natural starting line, but Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so each hour of difference between local time and home time equals 15° of longitude.
The most accurate early clocks relied on pendulums, which were useless on swaying ships.
Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offered rewards for finding longitude at sea; John Harrison, a self-taught clockmaker, built the H4 timekeeper, trialled on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761.

title: Captain Cook's Pacific voyages
description: James Cook's three voyages (1768-1779) charted New Zealand and Australia's east coast, crossed the Antarctic Circle, and relied on the K1 timekeeper.

facts.text: In 1768 James Cook sailed HMS Endeavour for Tahiti to observe the transit of Venus across the Sun.
In 1769 Cook opened secret Admiralty instructions to sail south in search of a great southern continent and to explore New Zealand.
On his first voyage (1768-1771) Cook charted the coast of New Zealand, showing it was not part of a southern continent, and in 1770 reached Australia's east coast.
On his second voyage (1772-1775), in January 1773, Cook became the first navigator to cross the Antarctic Circle, and by 1774 he had shown there was no habitable southern continent.
Cook's third voyage (1776-1779) searched for a Northwest Passage; in February 1779 he was killed at Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi.
Cook's second voyage carried K1, Larcum Kendall's copy of Harrison's H4; it performed so well that Cook came to rely on it.
In 1774 Cook accurately charted Easter Island (Rapa Nui), the Marquesas and other Pacific islands.

title: Tupaia, navigator of Raʻiatea
description: Tupaia, a navigator and priest from Raʻiatea, piloted Endeavour among the islands and drew a chart of 74 islands arranged by Polynesian sailing directions.

facts.text: Tupaia, a navigator, scholar and artist from Raʻiatea, chose to join Cook's voyage in 1769 and piloted Endeavour through the scattered islands south of Tahiti.
Tupaia drew a chart of 74 islands around Tahiti; rather than fixing positions the European way, it most likely showed the islands' relationships and sailing directions from Tahiti.
Despite his skill, Tupaia was often the subject of racism and derision from members of the crew; he died at Batavia in 1770.

title: The HMS Challenger expedition
description: HMS Challenger (1872-1876), a warship refitted with laboratories, sounded the ocean with weighted rope, including 4,475 fathoms in the Mariana Trench.

facts.text: The Royal Navy removed 15 of HMS Challenger's 17 guns and turned the space into laboratories and workrooms, making it the first dedicated oceanographic research vessel.
HMS Challenger left England in December 1872 and spent three and a half years at sea, crossing the Atlantic, Pacific and Southern Oceans.
Challenger measured depth by lowering a weighted rope to the sea floor, and carried dredging ropes more than 7 km long.
In 1875, in the Mariana Trench, Challenger's rope sounding reached 4,475 fathoms (8,184 m), the deepest point known at the time.
The trench's deepest spot is called Challenger Deep, named for a later survey ship, Challenger II, which surveyed the Mariana Trench in 1951.

title: Challenger proves the deep is alive
description: Many scientists doubted life could survive the deep; Challenger found more than 4,700 new species, and its 50-volume report founded oceanography.

facts.text: Before Challenger, many scientists doubted anything could survive the deep sea's pressure, cold and darkness; in the 1840s Edward Forbes argued that life ceased below a few hundred meters.
The Challenger expedition described more than 4,700 new species, showing that life exists under extreme pressure and total darkness in the deep sea.
Challenger's results filled a 50-volume report that took 23 years to compile, and the voyage is credited with giving birth to oceanography.

title: Diving bells
description: A diving bell is a container open at the bottom that traps air; Halley resupplied it with barrels of air and Smeaton added an air pump.

facts.text: Early diving bells were containers open only at the bottom, holding air; Aristotle mentioned a rudimentary diving bell.
A simple diving bell could not supply fresh air to keep a diver going for more than a few minutes.
Edmond Halley, who owned a diving company salvaging shipwrecks, sent fresh air down to his bell in barrels and let used air out through a stopcock.
In the late 18th century, British engineer John Smeaton fitted an air pump to the diving bell, making it fully practical.

title: The hard-hat diving helmet
description: Augustus Siebe's copper helmet, sealed to a waterproof suit and fed air by a hose from a surface pump, made hard-hat diving the standard for more than a century.

facts.text: In the 1830s Augustus Siebe developed a copper diving helmet sealed to a waterproof suit; air was pumped down a hose from the surface, a valve let breathed air out, and only the diver's hands were exposed.
In 1840 Siebe's diving suits were used to clear the wreck of HMS Royal George, establishing his design.
The US Navy's Mark V hard-hat diving helmet was in service from 1916 to 1984.
Hard-hat divers depended on crews on deck turning wheels to pump their air, and wore heavy weights to stay down.

title: Scuba and the demand regulator
description: The 1943 Aqua-Lung's demand regulator releases tank air only when the diver inhales, at the surrounding water pressure, freeing divers from hoses.

facts.text: A person cannot inhale surface air through a snorkel from about a meter down (below about 0.9 m, or even less), because of water pressure; to breathe deeper, a diver needs air under pressure that rises with depth.
In 1943 Jacques-Yves Cousteau and engineer Émile Gagnan co-invented the Aqua-Lung, the first truly self-contained underwater breathing apparatus (scuba), adapting a gas regulator Gagnan had designed.
The Aqua-Lung's demand regulator released only the air the diver needed, when they breathed in, at a pressure matching the surrounding water.

title: Scuba's pressure dangers
description: Air breathed at depth expands on ascent, so divers must exhale; extra nitrogen absorbed at depth can bubble out as the bends if they rise too fast.

facts.text: If a diver fills their lungs with compressed air at 10 m (33 feet) and rises without breathing out, that air doubles in volume and can overinflate and rupture the lungs.
The most common cause of lung injury in scuba diving is holding the breath while rising, so divers must breathe out freely during ascent.
Each breath at depth holds more gas molecules; the extra nitrogen builds up in blood and tissues and, if pressure falls too fast on ascent, forms bubbles: decompression sickness, the bends.
Divers prevent the bends by limiting depth, dive time and ascent speed, and many make a safety stop of a few minutes at about 4.5 m below the surface.

title: How submarines dive and surface
description: Submarines and submersibles flood ballast tanks with seawater to dive and blow them clear with compressed air, or drop weights, to rise.

facts.text: A submarine design from 1747 filled goatskin bags with water to submerge and forced the water out to rise, a forerunner of the modern ballast tank.
Submarines and submersibles flood ballast tanks with water to submerge; to resurface they drop ballast weights or blow the tanks clear of water with stored compressed air, becoming buoyant again.
With the right balance of water and air in a ballast tank, a craft can be made to float at any depth.

title: Nautilus and Alvin
description: USS Nautilus (1954) was the first nuclear-powered submarine and passed under the North Pole in 1958; the submersible Alvin (1964) has made more than 5,000 dives.

facts.text: USS Nautilus, commissioned in 1954, was the world's first nuclear-powered submarine, and a nuclear submarine could operate fully submerged at high speed indefinitely.
On August 3, 1958, USS Nautilus became the first ship to pass under the North Pole, traveling beneath the Arctic ice.
Alvin, commissioned in 1964 and operated by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, has carried researchers on more than 5,000 dives, with two scientists and a pilot aboard.
After upgrades completed in 2021, Alvin is rated to 6,500 m, which WHOI says gives researchers in-person access to 99% of the ocean floor.
Submersibles such as Alvin are deployed from a ship to the sea, unlike submarines that sail on their own.

title: Trieste reaches Challenger Deep
description: On January 23, 1960, Piccard and Walsh took the bathyscaphe Trieste, lifted by a gasoline float and sunk by iron ballast, to about 10,916 m.

facts.text: On January 23, 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy Lieutenant Don Walsh took the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of Challenger Deep.
Trieste hung from a float filled with gasoline, which is lighter than water and barely compresses under pressure.
To sink, a bathyscaphe carried heavy iron pellets as ballast, held by electromagnets; to rise, it released them.
Trieste's crew rode in a heavy steel cabin designed to resist the pressure of the deep.
Trieste's descent took nearly five hours; the crew spent about 20 minutes on the bottom, then dropped ballast for a rise of more than three hours.
Trieste reported reaching about 10,916 m (35,813 feet) in Challenger Deep.
At about 10,916 m, by the rule of one atmosphere per 10 m, the water adds roughly 1,090 atmospheres of pressure.

title: Returning to the deepest point
description: James Cameron dove solo to Challenger Deep in 2012; in 2019 Victor Vescovo's Limiting Factor became the first sub to reach the bottom more than once.

facts.text: On March 26, 2012, James Cameron piloted DEEPSEA CHALLENGER solo to Challenger Deep, the first person to reach the bottom since 1960.

Between April 28 and May 5, 2019, Victor Vescovo took the submersible Limiting Factor, built for repeated dives, to the bottom of Challenger Deep four times, the first time any submersible had gone there more than once.

title: Satellites measure the sea
description: Radar altimeters time pulses bounced off the sea to measure its height to a few centimeters; other sensors read surface temperature and color.

facts.text: Sea level is generally about 20 cm higher in the Pacific than in the Atlantic, because Pacific water is usually warmer, fresher and less dense.
A satellite radar altimeter sends pulses of radio waves to the sea surface and times how long they take to bounce back, which gives the height of the sea.
Sonar sends a pulse of sound into water and times its echo; a radar altimeter uses the same echo-timing idea with radio pulses from orbit.
Since TOPEX/Poseidon launched in 1992, a series of altimetry satellites has flown the same orbit, repeating it every ten days.
These satellites measure sea level to within a few centimeters for 90% of the world's oceans.
Satellites also measure sea surface temperature, which reveals upwelling and warm currents such as the Gulf Stream, and ocean color, used to spot algal blooms and forecast where they will drift.

title: Argo floats
description: Thousands of Argo floats drift about 1 km deep, dive to 2 km every ten days, rise measuring temperature and salinity, and send data by satellite.

facts.text: An Argo float drifts at about 1 km deep; every ten days it sinks to 2 km, then rises to the surface measuring temperature and salinity, and relays its data to satellites.
An Argo float changes depth by pumping oil between an internal reservoir and an external bladder.
The Argo program deploys thousands of floats across the world's ocean; its 3,000-float goal was reached in November 2007.
Argo is named after Jason's ship in Greek myth because the floats work alongside the Jason satellites that measure the ocean's surface.

title: Wayfinding returns to the sea
description: In 1980 Nainoa Thompson, taught by Mau Piailug, navigated Hōkūleʻa from Tahiti to Hawaiʻi without instruments, a feat not done in 600 years.

facts.text: In 1980, Nainoa Thompson navigated Hōkūleʻa from Tahiti back to Hawaiʻi without instruments, a feat the Polynesian Voyaging Society says had not been accomplished in 600 years; Mau Piailug sailed in support.

title: How fishing feeds the world
description: Fishing and fish farming produce a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals, a key protein source for 3.1 billion people.

facts.text: In 2024, fisheries and aquaculture produced a record 195 million tonnes of aquatic animals, such as fish, molluscs and crustaceans (FAO).
Aquatic animal foods available for eating came to about 21 kg per person worldwide in 2023 (FAO: 21.1 kg).
Aquatic animal foods supply at least one fifth of the animal protein eaten by 3.1 billion people (FAO, 2026).

title: Farms overtake the wild catch
description: The wild catch has been flat since the late 1980s; growth comes from aquaculture, which overtook capture fisheries in 2022.

facts.text: Since the late 1980s, the world's wild catch (capture fisheries) has stayed roughly flat, at about 86 to 94 million tonnes a year.
In 2024, capture fisheries caught 92 million tonnes of aquatic animals, 80 million tonnes of it from the sea.
In 2022, for the first time, aquaculture (farming fish, shellfish and other water animals) produced more aquatic animals than capture fisheries.
In 2024, aquaculture produced 103 million tonnes of aquatic animals, about 53% of the total.

title: Overfishing and the state of fish stocks
description: Overfishing means catching fish faster than they replace themselves; it collapsed Newfoundland's cod, and about three in eight stocks are overfished.

facts.text: NOAA defines overfishing as catching a stock faster than the rate that gives its maximum sustainable yield; in plain terms, faster than it can replace itself.
After decades of overfishing, Canada banned commercial northern cod fishing off Newfoundland on July 2, 1992, directly costing about 19,000 jobs.
The northern cod ban was expected to last two years but lasted 32; a cautious commercial cod fishery reopened in 2024.
In 2023, about 62% of assessed marine fish stocks were fished within biologically sustainable levels, so roughly three in eight were overfished (FAO).
Measured by catch, about 73% of 2023 landings came from sustainable stocks, because big stocks tend to be better managed (FAO).

title: How fisheries recover
description: Catch cuts and closed grounds let fish stocks rebuild, as North Atlantic swordfish did by 2009; NOAA counts 50 US stocks rebuilt since 2000.

facts.text: By the late 1990s the average swordfish caught in US waters weighed about 41 kg (90 lb), down from about 113 kg (250 lb) in the 1960s.
Under a 1999 international rebuilding plan, catches were cut and grounds closed to protect young swordfish; the North Atlantic stock was declared rebuilt in 2009, a year early.
NOAA's 2023 Status of Stocks report counted 50 US fish stocks rebuilt since 2000.

title: Ships carry world trade
description: Around 80% of international trade in goods by volume goes by sea, made cheap by standard containers since 1956.

facts.text: Around 80% of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea (UNCTAD).
In 1956, trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean's ship Ideal X carried 58 metal containers from Newark to Houston.
In 1956, loading a ship the conventional way cost more than $5.80 a ton; loading the Ideal X's containers cost about 16 cents a ton.

title: Shipping emissions and the net-zero debate
description: Shipping makes about 2.9% of greenhouse emissions; the IMO targets net zero by around 2050, but its Net-Zero Framework was delayed amid opposition.

facts.text: The IMO's Fourth GHG Study estimated that shipping made about 2.9% of global human-caused greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 (2.89%).
The IMO's 2023 greenhouse gas strategy aims for net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050.
In April 2025 IMO members approved a Net-Zero Framework (a fuel standard plus a price on emissions); in October 2025 they voted 57 to 49 to delay adopting it by a year.
The EU, Brazil and Pacific island nations backed the Net-Zero Framework; the United States, calling it a global carbon tax, and Saudi Arabia opposed it.

title: Oil from under the sea
description: Nearly 30% of the world's crude oil came from offshore wells in 2015, increasingly from deep water.

facts.text: In 2015, offshore wells in more than 50 countries supplied nearly 30% of the world's crude oil (EIA).
Most offshore oil comes from shallow water, which is cheaper and easier, but companies are drilling ever deeper, notably off Brazil and in the Gulf of Mexico.

title: Offshore wind
description: Strong, steady sea winds drive offshore wind farms, from Vindeby (1991) to floating turbines for deep water, raising questions about sharing the sea with fishers.

facts.text: The world's first offshore wind farm, Vindeby in Denmark, was built in 1991 with 11 turbines.
Winds at sea are strong and consistent, and offshore wind farms can be built near crowded coastal cities that need the power (US DOE).
About two-thirds of US offshore wind potential lies over water too deep for turbines fixed to the sea floor; those sites need floating platforms.
NOAA Fisheries notes offshore wind may push trawl and dredge fishers off traditional grounds, while marine life may cluster around turbine structures (a reef effect).

title: Where ocean pollution comes from
description: About 80% of ocean pollution comes from land, mostly as runoff; plastic leaks in by the millions of tonnes, and spills like Deepwater Horizon add oil.

facts.text: According to NOAA, about 80% of the pollution reaching the marine environment comes from the land.
Much ocean pollution is runoff: rain washes it off many small sources, like cars, farms and septic tanks; oil dripped by millions of engines reaches the sea.
UNEP estimates 19 to 23 million tonnes of plastic waste leak into lakes, rivers and seas every year.
In 2010 the Deepwater Horizon blowout killed 11 workers and spilled about 134 million gallons (about 507 million liters) of oil over 87 days, the largest US marine spill.

title: Dead zones
description: Nutrient runoff feeds algae whose decay uses up oxygen, creating dead zones such as the one in the Gulf of Mexico every summer.

facts.text: Excess nutrients feed algae; when the algae die and decompose, the rotting uses up oxygen, leaving a dead zone where most sea life dies or leaves.
A dead zone forms in the Gulf of Mexico each summer, fed by nutrients from farms and cities across the Mississippi-Atchafalaya River Basin.

title: Who controls the sea
description: The Law of the Sea gives coastal countries resource zones up to 200 nautical miles; the high seas beyond, nearly two-thirds of the ocean, gained a protection treaty in 2026.

facts.text: Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a coastal country controls natural resources in its exclusive economic zone, up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) out.
Beyond national zones lie the high seas; areas beyond national jurisdiction cover nearly two-thirds of the ocean.
The High Seas Treaty (BBNJ Agreement), under the Law of the Sea convention, entered into force on January 17, 2026, and lets countries create protected areas on the high seas.
As of April 2026, protected areas covered only about 1.66% of the high seas (IUCN).

title: Marine protected areas and the reserve debate
description: About 10% of the ocean is protected, toward a 30% goal; no-take reserves hold far more fish, though scientists debate how much they matter versus managing fished waters.

facts.text: A marine protected area gives part of the sea extra protection; many allow some fishing, while the strictest, no-take reserves, ban fishing and other extraction.
As of April 2026, about 10% of the ocean (10.01%) lay in protected and conserved areas (IUCN).
In 2022, countries agreed in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
A 2018 review by Enric Sala and Sylvaine Giakoumi found fish biomass in no-take reserves averaged 570% more than in unprotected waters (a corrected figure).
Fisheries scientist Ray Hilborn replied that the reserve estimate was too high and that real protection of sea life will come from how fished areas are managed.

title: What pirate life was really like
description: Golden-age pirates ran ships by codes and votes, and spent their loot rather than burying it; walking the plank is largely a myth.

facts.text: Walking the plank is largely a myth: Royal Museums Greenwich says pirates threw victims overboard or marooned them instead.
The so-called golden age of piracy lasted less than 50 years.
Many pirate captains adopted codes of conduct to run the ship fairly, and crews often voted for their captain and could remove a bad one.
One pirate code supposedly promised 800 pieces of eight to a man who lost a limb, with smaller amounts for lesser injuries.
Pirates almost never buried treasure: they mainly spent it quickly, and they made no treasure maps.
Captain William Kidd was a rare exception: treasure he hid on Gardiners Island, off Long Island, in 1699 was dug up and used as evidence at his trial.

title: Blackbeard, the real record
description: Blackbeard's flagship, a captured slave ship, sailed for barely seven months before grounding in 1718; he died that November, and the wreck was found in 1996.

facts.text: On November 28, 1717, Blackbeard's crew captured the French slave ship La Concorde, which became his flagship, Queen Anne's Revenge.
In June 1718, Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground entering what is now Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina, and was abandoned.
Blackbeard was killed on November 22, 1718, at Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina, by a force led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard.
In November 1996, the wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge was found in Beaufort Inlet, and archaeologists have studied it since.

title: Real animals behind sea monsters
description: Mermaid sightings were likely manatees and dugongs, and sea serpents likely giant oarfish: real animals glimpsed badly.

facts.text: On January 9, 1493, near today's Dominican Republic, Columbus wrote that he had seen three mermaids, not as beautiful as they are painted; they were most likely manatees.
Manatees and dugongs belong to the Sirenia, named after the Sirens of Greek myth; they are believed to be the basis of the mermaid myth.
The giant oarfish, the longest bony fish, reaches about 8 m and lives about 200 to 1,000 m deep; it tops the list of real sources for sea-serpent tales.
An oarfish at the surface is usually in trouble and stranding itself.

title: Monsters on the map
description: The 1539 Carta Marina filled northern seas with monsters, and kraken tales likely grew from washed-up remains of giant squid and octopuses.

facts.text: Olaus Magnus's Carta Marina, a large map of Scandinavia published in 1539, is famous for the sea monsters drawn in its waters.
Kraken tales were likely fed by rotted remains of giant squid and large octopuses washing up on beaches, which people tried to explain.

title: Practical ways to protect the ocean
description: Beach cleanups remove and count trash, and the counts show which rules work; cutting carbon dioxide emissions, the IPCC finds, tackles the main driver of surface ocean acidification.

facts.text: Since 1986, over 19 million volunteers in Ocean Conservancy's International Coastal Cleanup have collected over 400 million pounds (about 181 million kg) of trash.
Cleanup volunteers record every item they collect by type, and the tallies show which items to target and whether rules work.
After Washington, D.C., banned foam food containers in 2016, teams monitoring the Anacostia River saw less foam entering the water.
The IPCC concluded in 2021 that human-caused carbon dioxide emissions are, virtually certainly, the main driver of the surface open ocean's current acidification.

title: The plastics treaty debate
description: Global plastics treaty talks stalled in 2025 over whether to limit plastic production or focus on waste and recycling.

facts.text: In August 2025, talks in Geneva on a global plastics treaty ended without agreement; governments planned to resume negotiating later in 2026.
The High Ambition Coalition wants rules across plastic's whole life cycle, including production; the Like-Minded Countries, mostly oil producers, favor a focus on waste and recycling.
